Variance-Reduced Policy Gradient is Nearly Minimax-Optimal

 

Leonardo Cesani11 1 Correspondence to: leonardo.cesani@polimi.it.          Matteo Papini          Marcello Restelli

Politecnico di Milano          Università degli Studi di Milano          Politecnico di Milano

Abstract

Standard Policy Gradient (PG) algorithms suffer from high estimation variance because they rely on Monte Carlo updates. While off-policy variance reduction mitigates this problem, establishing optimal sample complexity currently requires either restrictive assumptions, such as uniformly bounded importance weights, or impractical second-order operations. In this work, we introduce Loopless Variance-Reduced PG (LVR-PG), a unified theoretical framework that abstracts a class of first-order estimators that integrate recursive updates with defensive importance sampling, including known estimators such as PAGE-PG and STORM-PG. We prove that this algorithmic class achieves 𝒪~​(ϵ−2)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-2}) last-iterate global convergence under weak gradient domination for general parametric policies. We establish this guarantee using purely first-order updates, with minimal assumptions and without gradient preconditioners. By extending state-of-the-art lower bounds to continuous parametric policies, we establish an Ω⁡(ϵ−2)\Omega(\epsilon^{-2}) sample complexity limit, confirming our framework is minimax-optimal up to logarithmic factors and horizon terms.

1 Introduction

In recent years, Reinforcement Learning (Sutton et al., 1998, RL, ) has been used as the central tool for aligning and scaling the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (Brown et al., 2020; Achiam et al., 2023, LLMs, ). Methods based on Proximal Policy Optimization (Schulman et al., 2017; Ouyang et al., 2022, PPO,) and, more recently, Group Relative Policy Optimization (Shao et al., 2024, GRPO, ) have achieved enormous success on reasoning tasks (Guo et al., 2025) and aligning model outputs with human preferences (Ziegler et al., 2019; Bai et al., 2022). At their core, the algorithms powering these methods reduce to the Policy Gradient (Deisenroth et al., 2013, PG, ) framework.

Despite the empirical success, their learning efficiency is a matter of debate (Rafailov et al., 2023). Standard PG methods estimate the gradient of the expected return using sampled trajectories (Sutton et al., 1999), and the resulting Monte Carlo estimates can exhibit high estimation variance (Zhao et al., 2011). Actor-critic algorithms (Konda and Tsitsiklis, 2000) address this difficulty through a learned critic, whose approximation error can introduce bias. For LLMs, maintaining and updating an additional critic also entails substantial memory and computational costs, motivating actor-only methods that avoid a separate critic network (Yuan et al., 2023; Ahmadian et al., 2024). Improving trajectory efficiency without introducing a learned critic is therefore relevant to scalable policy optimization.

Reducing gradient-estimation variance has long motivated theoretical research on the sample complexity of PG methods, defined as the number of trajectories nn required to learn an ϵ\epsilon-optimal policy, where ϵ\epsilon is the required accuracy. Recent actor-only applications give this established problem renewed practical relevance. A central theoretical objective is to determine whether purely first-order, actor-only methods can achieve the optimal Ω⁡(ϵ−2)\Omega(\epsilon^{-2}) sample-complexity lower bound (Azar et al., 2013). However, the existing guarantees for such methods do not match this lower bound and require additional assumptions on the Hessian of the log-policy or on the variance of the importance weights.

Within the class of actor-only PG methods, variance reduction seeks to improve sample complexity by reusing historical gradient information while retaining gradient-only updates. Unlike in standard stochastic optimization, the trajectory distribution depends on the policy parameters and therefore changes over the course of optimization. To account for this distribution shift, these methods employ Importance Sampling (IS), weighting trajectory-based estimates by likelihood ratios between the target and sampling policies. Inspired by stochastic non-convex optimization, early methods such as SVR-PG (Papini et al., 2018) and SRVR-PG (Xu et al., 2019) employ double-loop architectures. These compute large-batch gradient estimates at a fixed anchor policy to correct subsequent inner-loop mini-batch updates, making the refresh schedule dependent on the chosen epoch length. Loopless methods instead incorporate historical information through recursive momentum updates or probabilistic refreshes, as in STORM-PG (Yuan et al., 2020; Ding et al., 2022) and PAGE-PG (Gargiani et al., 2022), respectively.

Existing analyses of these importance-sampling-based methods impose strong statistical assumptions, notably a uniform bound on the variance of Importance Weights (IW) (Liu et al., 2020; Ding et al., 2022). This condition is not generally guaranteed in continuous state-action spaces, where trajectory-level likelihood ratios accumulate the distribution shifts induced by policy updates. Paczolay et al. (2024) addresses this by using defensive IS (Owen and Zhou, 2000), but it only studies convergence to a first-order stationary point. In contrast, N-PG-IGT (Fatkhullin et al., 2023) circumvents the IW assumption through implicit gradient transport, retaining historical gradient information without using importance sampling. Its established sample complexity of 𝒪~​(ϵ−2.5)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-2.5}), however, does not attain the optimal accuracy dependence. Other approaches attain this dependence through different information mechanisms. HARPG uses Hessian-vector products (Fatkhullin et al., 2023), whereas ANPG estimates natural-gradient directions through an auxiliary stochastic optimization problem involving Fisher geometry (Mondal and Aggarwal, 2024). Despite their theoretical appeal, these approaches require additional computational overhead beyond policy-gradient estimation, motivating the study of gradient-only methods. Their analyses also impose regularity assumptions on policy derivatives, as summarized in Table 1.

The question is therefore whether existing gradient-only PG methods can achieve last-iterate global convergence with the optimal accuracy dependence, without assuming uniformly bounded importance-weight variance or additional second-order regularity.

Original Contributions.

We study a unified theoretical framework encompassing existing gradient-only PG estimators equipped with defensive IS. In the remainder of the paper, we present our main contributions as follows:

  • •

    In Section 3, we adapt the hard-instance construction of Azar et al. (2013) to continuously parameterized policies satisfying WGD, establishing that any algorithm guaranteeing expected ϵ\epsilon-optimality requires Ω⁡(ϵ−2)\Omega(\epsilon^{-2}) trajectories in the worst-case.

  • •

    In Section 4, we introduce the unified LVR-PG framework, abstracting loopless estimators like PAGE-PG (Gargiani et al., 2022) and STORM-PG (Yuan et al., 2020). By integrating defensive importance sampling (Paczolay et al., 2024) to control off-policy variance, we avoid assumptions on the variance of the importance weights.

  • •

    In Section 5, we prove LVR-PG achieves last-iterate global convergence with a sample complexity of 𝒪~​(ϵ−2)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-2}), matching our lower bound up to logarithmic factors, without assuming uniformly bounded importance-weight variance or additional second-order regularity.

  • •

    In Section 6, we empirically benchmark the LVR-PG framework against state-of-the-art baselines, identifying the defensive variant of STORM-PG as the dominant algorithmic configuration with superior sample efficiency. The full experimental evaluation is provided in Appendix I.

2 Preliminaries

Notation.

For a measurable set 𝒳\mathcal{X}, we denote by Δ𝒳\Delta_{\mathcal{X}} the set of probability measures over 𝒳\mathcal{X}. For P∈Δ𝒳P\in\Delta_{\mathcal{X}}, if it admits a density, we denote it by pp. We will use x∼Px\sim P to express that the random variable xx is distributed according to PP. For n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, we let ⟦n⟧≔{1,…,n}\llbracket n\rrbracket\coloneqq\{1,\dots,n\}. Vectors are indicated with bold letters. Given two symmetric matrices AA and BB, we say that A⪰BA\succeq B if the matrix A−BA-B is positive semidefinite.

Interaction Protocol.

We consider an agent interacting with a Markov Decision Process (Puterman, 2014, MDP, ) ℳ=(𝒮,𝒜,p,r,ρ0,γ)\mathcal{M}=\left(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},p,r,\rho_{0},\gamma\right) over independent, indefinite-length episodes. In each timestep h=0,1,…h=0,1,\dots, the agent observes a state 𝒔h∈𝒮⊆ℝd𝒮\bm{s}_{h}\in\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathcal{S}}}, where 𝒔0∼ρ0\bm{s}_{0}\sim\rho_{0} is the initial state and ρ0∈Δ𝒮\rho_{0}\in\Delta_{\mathcal{S}} is the initial-state distribution, and executes an action 𝒂h∈𝒜⊆ℝd𝒜\bm{a}_{h}\in\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathcal{A}}} sampled from a parametric stochastic policy π𝜽:𝒮→Δ𝒜\pi_{\bm{\theta}}:\mathcal{S}\rightarrow\Delta_{\mathcal{A}}. Here, 𝜽∈Θ⊆ℝdΘ\bm{\theta}\in\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_{\Theta}} is the parameter vector defining the policy space ΠΘ={π𝜽∣𝜽∈Θ}\Pi_{\Theta}=\{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}\mid\bm{\theta}\in\Theta\}. The agent then receives a reward rh+1≔r⁡(𝒔h,𝒂h)∈[−Rmax,Rmax]r_{h+1}\coloneqq r(\bm{s}_{h},\bm{a}_{h})\in[-R_{\max},R_{\max}] and transitions to a next state 𝒔h+1∼p(⋅∣𝒔h,𝒂h)∈Δ𝒮\bm{s}_{h+1}\sim p(\cdot\mid\bm{s}_{h},\bm{a}_{h})\in\Delta_{\mathcal{S}}. For a discount factor γ∈[0,1)\gamma\in[0,1), the performance of 𝜽\bm{\theta} is assessed via the expected discounted return under the assumption that 𝜽↦π𝜽\bm{\theta}\mapsto\pi_{\bm{\theta}} is differentiable. The latter is defined as:

J⁡(𝜽)≔𝔼⁡[∑h≥0γh​r​(𝒔h,𝒂h)|π𝜽],\displaystyle J(\bm{\theta})\coloneqq\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{h\geq 0}\gamma^{h}r(\bm{s}_{h},\bm{a}_{h})\,\bigg|\,\pi_{\bm{\theta}}\right],

where the expectation is taken over the trajectory distribution induced by the policy and the environment dynamics. In the following, we will refer to J:Θ→ℝJ:\Theta\rightarrow\mathbb{R} as the performance function, which is generally non-convex. Because the per-step rewards are bounded, it satisfies |J⁡(𝜽)|≤Rmax/(1−γ)|J(\bm{\theta})|\leq R_{\max}/(1-\gamma) for all 𝜽∈Θ\bm{\theta}\in\Theta. We denote the optimal performance as J∗≔max𝜽∈Θ⁡J⁡(𝜽)J^{*}\coloneqq\max_{\bm{\theta}\in\Theta}J(\bm{\theta}).

Policy Gradients.

We consider learning algorithms that iteratively update a sequence of policies π𝜽1,…,π𝜽K\pi_{\bm{\theta}_{1}},\dots,\pi_{\bm{\theta}_{K}}. At each iteration kk, the agent collects a dataset 𝒟k={τ1k,…,τnkk}\mathcal{D}_{k}=\{\tau_{1}^{k},\dots,\tau^{k}_{n_{k}}\} of nkn_{k} independent trajectories drawn from the trajectory distribution induced by the policy p𝜽k​(τ)p_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}(\tau). To accommodate structural or safety constraints common in practical applications, we consider PG methods that restrict the parameter space to a closed convex set Θ⊆ℝdΘ\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_{\Theta}} and, similarly to Xu et al. (2019), update the parameters via projected stochastic gradient ascent: 𝜽k+1←𝒫Θ​(𝜽k+η​∇^𝜽​J​(𝜽k))\bm{\theta}_{k+1}\leftarrow\mathcal{P}_{\Theta}\left(\bm{\theta}_{k}+\eta\widehat{\nabla}_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k})\right). Here, η>0\eta>0 is the learning rate, and ∇^𝜽​J​(𝜽k)\widehat{\nabla}_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k}) is an unbiased estimator of the true gradient ∇𝜽J​(𝜽k)\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k}). We formalize the optimization geometry over the parameter domain Θ\Theta using the generalized gradient mapping 𝒢η(𝜽)≔1η(𝒫Θ(𝜽+η∇J(𝜽))−𝜽)\mathcal{G}_{\eta}(\bm{\theta})\coloneqq\frac{1}{\eta}\left(\mathcal{P}_{\Theta}(\bm{\theta}+\eta\nabla J(\bm{\theta}))-\bm{\theta}\right). This mapping acts as the projected gradient at 𝜽\bm{\theta}, recovering the standard gradient ∇𝜽J​(𝜽)\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}) in the unconstrained case Θ=ℝdΘ\Theta=\mathbb{R}^{d_{\Theta}}. To compute the stochastic gradient estimator ∇^𝜽​J​(𝜽)\widehat{\nabla}_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}) from finite interaction data without introducing approximation or truncation bias, we evaluate the infinite-horizon discounted objective using a randomized geometric stopping rule, in which the interaction with the environment is terminated after each transition with probability 1−γ1-\gamma, independently of the interaction history. For each trajectory τi\tau_{i}, let Hγ,i∈{1,2,…}H_{\gamma,i}\in\{1,2,\ldots\} denote the number of executed transitions, with stopping randomness independent across trajectories. In this way, the expected length of each trajectory is 𝔼⁡[Hγ,i]=(1−γ)−1\mathbb{E}[H_{\gamma,i}]=(1-\gamma)^{-1}, and, since Pr⁡(Hγ,i>h)=γh\Pr(H_{\gamma,i}>h)=\gamma^{h}, the expected undiscounted return accumulated before stopping matches the infinite-horizon discounted objective function J⁡(𝜽)J(\bm{\theta}). For theoretical analysis, we adopt the geometric stopping rule to obtain unbiased estimates of the infinite-horizon objective. In the empirical evaluation, we use a fixed horizon. Using the geometric horizons Hγ,iH_{\gamma,i}, the estimate ∇^𝜽​J​(𝜽k)\widehat{\nabla}_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k}) is computed from the on-policy dataset 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k} via the GPOMDP (Baxter and Bartlett, 2001) estimator:

∇^𝜽​J​(𝜽k)\displaystyle\widehat{\nabla}_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k}) =1nk​∑i=1nk𝒈⁡(τi∣𝜽k),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n_{k}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{k}}\bm{g}(\tau_{i}\mid\bm{\theta}_{k}), (1)
𝒈⁡(τi∣𝜽)\displaystyle\bm{g}(\tau_{i}\mid\bm{\theta}) ≔∑h=0Hγ,i−1(∑l=0h∇𝜽​log​π𝜽​(𝒂l∣𝒔l))​rh+1.\displaystyle\coloneqq\sum_{h=0}^{H_{\gamma,i}-1}\left(\sum_{l=0}^{h}\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{a}_{l}\mid\bm{s}_{l})\right)r_{h+1}.

While the variance of this on-policy estimator is bounded under standard regularity conditions (Zhao et al., 2011; Papini et al., 2022), it is often very large in practice, compromising learning efficiency.

Off-Policy Gradient Estimation.

To mitigate large variance of the estimator, variance-reduced algorithms reuse historical data to improve sample efficiency, requiring the evaluation of the gradient at a target policy 𝜽\bm{\theta} using trajectories collected by a different behavioral policy 𝜽′\bm{\theta}^{\prime}. To maintain an unbiased gradient estimate, these methods rely on Importance Sampling (Metelli et al., 2020, IS, ). Given a trajectory τ∼p(⋅∣𝜽′)\tau\sim p(\cdot\mid\bm{\theta}^{\prime}), the off-policy GPOMDP estimator is defined as ∇^𝜽​J​(𝜽)=1n​∑i=1nω⁡(𝜽,τi)​𝒈​(τi∣𝜽)\widehat{\nabla}_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\omega(\bm{\theta},\tau_{i})\bm{g}(\tau_{i}\mid\bm{\theta}), where ω⁡(𝜽,τi)\omega(\bm{\theta},\tau_{i}) is the importance weight defined by the trajectory density ratio:

ω⁡(𝜽,τi)≔p𝜽​(τi)p𝜽′​(τi)=∏h=0Hγ,i−1π𝜽​(𝒂h∣𝒔h)π𝜽′​(𝒂h∣𝒔h),\displaystyle\omega(\bm{\theta},\tau_{i})\coloneqq\frac{p_{\bm{\theta}}(\tau_{i})}{p_{\bm{\theta}^{\prime}}(\tau_{i})}=\prod_{h=0}^{H_{\gamma,i}-1}\frac{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{a}_{h}\mid\bm{s}_{h})}{\pi_{\bm{\theta}^{\prime}}(\bm{a}_{h}\mid\bm{s}_{h})},

where the environment transition dynamics and the trajectory’s stopping probability cancel out. While this off-policy estimator is unbiased, its variance scales with the χ2\chi^{2}-divergence between the trajectory distributions induced by 𝜽\bm{\theta} and 𝜽′\bm{\theta}^{\prime} (Cortes et al., 2010). Since the χ2\chi^{2}-divergence is generally unbounded, the importance-weight variance can easily diverge even for simple continuous policy classes, such as Gaussians (Zhang et al., 2021).

3 Learning Framework

To study the sample complexity of learning a globally optimal policy, we must define the structural and geometric properties of the objective landscape and establish the statistical limits of policy optimization.

Assumptions.

To study variance-reduced PG algorithms within a unified framework, we define the structural and geometric properties of the objective landscape that we will use in our analysis. First, we enforce the following standard regularity conditions on the policy parametrization.

Assumption 3.1 (Regularity).

The policy class admits finite constants C1,LS>0C_{1},L_{S}>0 such that, for all 𝛉,𝛉′∈Θ\bm{\theta},\bm{\theta}^{\prime}\in\Theta, and for any 𝐬∈𝒮\bm{s}\in\mathcal{S}, we have:

(i)​sup𝒂∈𝒜‖∇𝜽​log​π𝜽​(𝒂∣𝒔)‖2≤C1​,\displaystyle\textit{(i)}~~\sup_{\bm{a}\in\mathcal{A}}\big\|\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{a}\mid\bm{s})\big\|_{2}\leq C_{1}\textbf{},
(ii)​𝔼𝒂∼π𝜽[‖∇𝜽​log​π𝜽​(𝒂∣𝒔)−∇𝜽​log​π𝜽′​(𝒂∣𝒔)‖22]\displaystyle\textit{(ii)}~\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{\bm{a}\sim\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}\left[\big\|\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{a}\mid\bm{s})-\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}^{\prime}}(\bm{a}\mid\bm{s})\big\|_{2}^{2}\right]
≤LS2​‖𝜽−𝜽′‖22.\displaystyle\quad\quad\leq L_{S}^{2}\|\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}^{\prime}\|_{2}^{2}.

Assumption 3.1 (ii), introduced by Paczolay et al. (2024), relaxes the uniform Lipschitz score condition standard in prior literature (Papini et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2019; Yuan et al., 2020; Gargiani et al., 2022; Fatkhullin et al., 2023) by requiring only mean-squared smoothness under the on-policy distribution, rather than a worst-case bound across all state-action pairs. Condition (i) requires bounded score gradients, which softmax policies satisfy, for example. Under these regularity conditions, the performance function J⁡(𝜽)J(\bm{\theta}) and its stochastic gradient estimator are smooth and have bounded variance, respectively, as formalized in the following proposition (proof in Appendix D).

Proposition 3.1.

Under Assumption 3.1, the following properties hold.

(i)​𝕍​ar​(𝒈⁡(τ∣𝜽))≤4​Rmax2​C12(1−γ)3≕ν2;\displaystyle\textit{(i)}~~\mathbb{V}\text{ar}\left(\bm{g}(\tau\mid\bm{\theta})\right)\leq\frac{4R_{\max}^{2}C_{1}^{2}}{(1-\gamma)^{3}}\eqqcolon\nu^{2};
(ii)​‖∇𝜽2​J​(𝜽)‖2≤Rmax​(C12+LS)(1−γ)2≕L.\displaystyle\textit{(ii)}~\|\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}^{2}J(\bm{\theta})\|_{2}\leq\frac{R_{\max}(C_{1}^{2}+L_{S})}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}\eqqcolon L.

Finally, to ensure global convergence and prevent the learning trajectory from getting trapped in suboptimal solutions, we impose a standard geometric assumption on the objective landscape (Yuan et al., 2022; Montenegro et al., 2024).

Assumption 3.2 (Weak Gradient Domination (WGD)).

There exist χ>0\chi>0 and ψ≥0\psi\geq 0 such that, for every 𝛉∈Θ\bm{\theta}\in\Theta and a step size η≤1/L\eta\leq 1/L, it holds that:

J∗−J⁡(𝜽)≤χ​‖𝒢η​(𝜽)‖2+ψ\displaystyle J^{*}-J(\bm{\theta})\leq\chi\|\mathcal{G}_{\eta}(\bm{\theta})\|_{2}+\psi

Assumption 3.2 is the standard for global convergence of constrained stochastic optimization (Yuan et al., 2022; Masiha et al., 2022; Ding et al., 2022; Fatkhullin et al., 2023; Montenegro et al., 2024). Note that in the unconstrained setting, where Θ=ℝdΘ\Theta=\mathbb{R}^{d_{\Theta}}, the mapping strictly recovers the true gradient 𝒢η​(𝜽)=∇𝜽J​(𝜽)\mathcal{G}_{\eta}(\bm{\theta})=\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}), meaning this condition reduces to the standard WGDassumption on the gradient norm. When ψ=0\psi=0, we recover the (strong) gradient domination (GD) property: J∗−J⁡(𝜽)≤χ​‖𝒢η​(𝜽)‖2J^{*}-J(\bm{\theta})\leq\chi\|\mathcal{G}_{\eta}(\bm{\theta})\|_{2}. GD is stricter than WGD since it requires that the constrained performance function J⁡(𝜽)J(\bm{\theta}) has no suboptimal stationary points within the feasible domain. Instead, WGD admits local maxima as long as their performance is ψ\psi-close to the global optimum (Montenegro et al., 2024).

Lower Bound for Policy Optimization.

Having established the learning framework, we now investigate the statistical limits of the policy optimization problem.

Theorem 3.1 (Sample Complexity Lower Bound).

For any discount factor γ∈[2/3,1)\gamma\in[2/3,1) and sufficiently small target accuracy 0<ϵ<𝒪⁡(Rmaxγ⁡(1−γ))0<\epsilon<\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{R_{\max}}{\gamma(1-\gamma)}\right), there exists a class of MDPs ℳ\mathcal{M} and a policy parametrization satisfying Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2, such that any algorithm guaranteeing an expected sub-optimality gap J∗−𝔼⁡[J⁡(𝛉K)]≤ϵJ^{*}-\mathbb{E}[J(\bm{\theta}_{K})]\leq\epsilon must collect a number of trajectories nn satisfying:

n\displaystyle n =Ω⁡(Rmax2(1−γ)2​ϵ−2).\displaystyle=\Omega\left(\frac{R_{\max}^{2}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}\epsilon^{-2}\right).

Theorem 3.1 establishes an Ω⁡(ϵ−2)\Omega(\epsilon^{-2}) statistical barrier under our regularity and WGD assumptions. In the context of RL, however, our result shows that these geometric properties do not trivialize the learning problem. Even when WGD holds with zero bias, so that GD excludes suboptimal stationary points, it cannot eliminate the irreducible estimation variance induced by the stochastic transition dynamics, thereby preserving the Ω⁡(ϵ−2)\Omega(\epsilon^{-2}) statistical barrier. This accuracy dependence is consistent with variance-reduced stochastic optimization under GD, where an 𝒪⁡(ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}) sample complexity is achievable Fatkhullin et al. (2022).

However, existing lower bounds do not directly show this barrier in our setting. First, lower bounds for bounded-variance stochastic-gradient oracles concern algorithms that observe stochastic gradients Masiha et al. (2026), whereas MDP interaction provides additional information through states, actions, and rewards, enabling importance-weighted gradient evaluations across different policies using the same trajectories. Second, the tabular lower bound of Azar et al. (2013) does not automatically apply after restricting the MDP and policy class to satisfy GD. Theorem 3.1 addresses these limitations by establishing an Ω⁡(ϵ−2)\Omega(\epsilon^{-2}) sample complexity lower bound for policy optimization under the stated regularity and WGD assumptions.

Finally, Theorem 3.1 establishes a statistical limit for policy optimization, independently of the update rule. Although existing methods achieve near-optimal sample complexity using Hessian or Fisher information, the lower bound does not imply that such information is necessary to reach this statistical limit.

Matching the Lower Bound.

Theorem 3.1 establishes the statistical limit, leaving open whether first-order policy optimization methods attain the optimal accuracy dependence. In non-convex stochastic optimization under WGD, Masiha et al. (2026) establishes an Ω⁡(ϵ−3)\Omega(\epsilon^{-3}) lower bound for the gradient-only, bounded-variance oracle model. Improving this dependence requires additional oracle structure, which recursive variance-reduction methods exploit through “double sampling”: gradient evaluations at distinct parameters using shared randomness. In PG, implementing this coupling requires correcting the distribution shift induced by policy updates. Alternative approaches avoid importance sampling: N-PG-IGT provides a 𝒪~​(ϵ−2.5)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-2.5}) guarantee, whereas HARPG and ANPG attain the ϵ−2\epsilon^{-2} dependence through Hessian-vector products and Fisher geometry, respectively (Fatkhullin et al., 2023; Mondal and Aggarwal, 2024). We therefore investigate whether we can establish the optimal accuracy dependence of this first-order recursive framework without relying on Hessian-vector products or Fisher-based updates, potentially without assuming uniformly bounded importance-weight variance.

4 The LVR-PG Framework

To address the limitations identified in Section 3, we introduce Loopless Variance-Reduced Policy Gradient (LVR-PG), a unified framework for analyzing loopless, gradient-only PG estimators. By suitably setting its parameters, LVR-PG recovers state-of-the-art estimators such as STORM-PG (Yuan et al., 2020) and PAGE-PG (Gargiani et al., 2022), equipped with the defensive IS scheme of Paczolay et al. (2024), bounding the IW and removing the need to assume their variance to be uniformly bounded. Our goal is to establish that, with an appropriate choice of hyperparameters, an algorithm within LVR-PG achieves last-iterate global convergence with a sample complexity matching the Ω⁡(ϵ−2)\Omega(\epsilon^{-2}) lower bound of Theorem 3.1, up to logarithmic factors and horizon terms.

Defensive Importance Sampling

Classical variance-reduced PG evaluates past policies using on-policy data, leading to IW to diverge exponentially over the trajectory horizon. To avoid this blow-up in the IW, we sample trajectories from a mixture trajectory distribution and employ defensive IS (Owen and Zhou, 2000; Paczolay et al., 2024). Let p𝜽​(τ)p_{\bm{\theta}}(\tau) be the probability density of a trajectory τ\tau induced by a policy π𝜽\pi_{\bm{\theta}}. During off-policy estimation at iteration kk, the algorithm collects a mini-batch of BB trajectories. Instead of drawing these exclusively from the current policy, each trajectory is independently drawn from the target policy π𝜽k+1\pi_{\bm{\theta}_{k+1}} with probability ξ∈[0,1]\xi\in[0,1] and from the previous policy π𝜽k\pi_{\bm{\theta}_{k}} with probability 1−ξ1-\xi. This yields a mixture trajectory distribution, defined as qξ​(τ)=ξ​p𝜽k+1​(τ)+(1−ξ)​p𝜽k​(τ)q_{\xi}(\tau)=\xi p_{\bm{\theta}_{k+1}}(\tau)+(1-\xi)p_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}(\tau). To estimate the gradient at either 𝜽k+1\bm{\theta}_{k+1} or 𝜽k\bm{\theta}_{k} using trajectories sampled from qξq_{\xi}, we use the defensive IS weight ωξ​(𝜽,τ)≔p𝜽​(τ)/qξ​(τ)\omega_{\xi}(\bm{\theta},\tau)\coloneqq p_{\bm{\theta}}(\tau)/q_{\xi}(\tau), where 𝜽∈{𝜽k+1,𝜽k}\bm{\theta}\in\{\bm{\theta}_{k+1},\bm{\theta}_{k}\}. For ξ∈(0,1)\xi\in(0,1), each target trajectory density enters qξq_{\xi} with a positive coefficient, so its importance weight is bounded by the reciprocal of that coefficient. In particular, when evaluating the current policy, we have ωξ​(𝜽k+1,τ)≤1/ξ\omega_{\xi}(\bm{\theta}_{k+1},\tau)\leq 1/\xi, and similarly ωξ​(𝜽k,τ)≤1/(1−ξ)\omega_{\xi}(\bm{\theta}_{k},\tau)\leq 1/(1-\xi). One can easily show that the gradient estimate computed using this mixture distribution remains unbiased.

The Unified Estimator.

Building upon the loopless variance reduction principles introduced in Yuan et al. (2020) and Gargiani et al. (2022), our framework regulates full-batch and mini-batch updates through a randomized mechanism governed by p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1], which we call refresh probability parameter. At iteration k∈⟦K⟧k\in\llbracket K\rrbracket, the evaluation of the target policy 𝜽k+1\bm{\theta}_{k+1} and the construction of the new gradient estimator ∇^𝜽†​J​(𝜽k+1)\widehat{\nabla}^{\dagger}_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k+1}) depend on a Bernoulli realization ck∼ℬ⁡(p)c_{k}\sim\mathcal{B}(p). If ck=1c_{k}=1, the framework executes a full refresh, sampling NN trajectories directly from the target policy π𝜽k+1\pi_{\bm{\theta}_{k+1}} to compute a full-batch gradient estimate with Equation (1) with nk=Nn_{k}=N. If ck=0c_{k}=0, the framework bypasses the full-batch estimation in favor of a recursive mini-batch update. To evaluate the gradients of both π𝜽k+1\pi_{\bm{\theta}_{k+1}} and π𝜽k\pi_{\bm{\theta}_{k}} simultaneously, LVR-PG collects B≪NB\ll N trajectories independently drawn from the mixture behavior distribution qξq_{\xi}. This allows us to compute the Defensive IS operator ωξ​(𝜽,τ)\omega_{\xi}(\bm{\theta},\tau) via the density ratio. Using this mini-batch and the mixture IS operator, the gradient estimator is recursively updated using a momentum parameter α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1] to control off-policy variance:

∇^𝜽†​J​(𝜽k+1)=𝒈Bωξ​(𝜽k+1)+(1−α)​[∇^𝜽†​J​(𝜽k)−𝒈Bωξ​(𝜽k)],\begin{split}\widehat{\nabla}^{\dagger}_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k+1})&=\bm{g}_{B}^{\omega_{\xi}}(\bm{\theta}_{k+1})\\ &\quad+(1-\alpha)\left[\widehat{\nabla}^{\dagger}_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k})-\bm{g}_{B}^{\omega_{\xi}}(\bm{\theta}_{k})\right],\end{split} (2)

where 𝒈Bωξ​(𝜽)≔1B​∑i=1Bωξ​(𝜽,τi)​𝒈​(τi∣𝜽)\bm{g}_{B}^{\omega_{\xi}}(\bm{\theta})\coloneqq\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\omega_{\xi}(\bm{\theta},\tau_{i})\bm{g}(\tau_{i}\mid\bm{\theta}). The momentum parameter α\alpha regulates the degree to which past gradient errors are discounted, and enables to control of the variance-reduction strategy to use: setting α=0\alpha=0 and p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1] recovers the update rule of PAGE-PG (Gargiani et al., 2022), while setting α>0\alpha>0 yields the momentum update of STORM-PG (Yuan et al., 2020). In the rest of the paper, we will refer to the defensive versions of these two algorithms as DEF-PAGE-PG and DEF-STORM-PG, respectively. Finally, once we compute the variance-reduced estimator ∇^𝜽†​J​(𝜽k)\widehat{\nabla}_{\bm{\theta}}^{\dagger}J(\bm{\theta}_{k}), we update the policy parameters via projected stochastic gradient ascent. The algorithm aims to find a parameter 𝜽∈Θ\bm{\theta}\in\Theta that maximizes the performance function subject to this constraint.

5 Convergence and Optimality

In this section, we establish the sample complexity required by an instantiation of the LVR-PG framework to obtain an ϵ\epsilon-approximate global optimum. Specifically, we demonstrate that the LVR-PG framework defines a class of minimax–optimal first-order algorithms, up to logarithmic factors. The proofs for the results presented in this section are deferred to Appendix E.

Theorem 5.1 (Global Convergence of LVR-PG).

Under Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2, for any target accuracy ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and fixed mini-batch size B≥1B\geq 1, let the batch sizes be N,N0=Θ⁡(ϵ−2)N,N_{0}=\Theta(\epsilon^{-2}) and the learning rate be η=Θ⁡(B​ϵ)\eta=\Theta(B\epsilon). For appropriately chosen hyperparameters satisfying p,α=𝒪⁡(B​ϵ2)p,\alpha=\mathcal{O}(B\epsilon^{2}) and p+α=Ω⁡(B​ϵ2)p+\alpha=\Omega(B\epsilon^{2}) and choosing ξ=1/2\xi=1/2, LVR-PG guarantees an expected suboptimality gap J∗−𝔼⁡[J⁡(𝛉K)]≤ψ+ϵJ^{*}-\mathbb{E}[J(\bm{\theta}_{K})]\leq\psi+\epsilon with a total expected sample complexity of at most:

n=𝒪~​(χ3​Rmax2(1−γ)4​ϵ2),\displaystyle n=\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\frac{\chi^{3}R_{\max}^{2}}{(1-\gamma)^{4}\epsilon^{2}}\right),

where 𝒪~​(⋅)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\cdot) hides logarithmic factors.

Proof Sketch.

The proof establishes the minimax-optimal sample complexity for LVR-PG by coupling the policy’s suboptimality descent with the variance recurrence of the gradient estimator.

Part I: The Descent Mechanics. We begin by characterizing the estimation error Δk≔𝔼⁡[‖∇^𝜽†​J​(𝜽k)−∇𝜽J​(𝜽k)‖22]\Delta_{k}\coloneqq\mathbb{E}[\|\widehat{\nabla}^{\dagger}_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k})-\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k})\|_{2}^{2}]. Lemma D.4 quantifies how this error propagates through recursive updates. Letting λ≔1−(1−p)​(1−α)2\lambda\coloneqq 1-(1-p)(1-\alpha)^{2} and Ψk≔𝔼⁡[‖𝜽k+1−𝜽k‖22]\Psi_{k}\coloneqq\mathbb{E}\left[\|\bm{\theta}_{k+1}-\bm{\theta}_{k}\|_{2}^{2}\right] we have:

Δk+1≤(1−λ)​Δk+2​(1−λ)​C†,ωB​Ψk+Cν.\displaystyle\Delta_{k+1}\leq(1-\lambda)\Delta_{k}+\frac{2(1-\lambda)C_{\dagger,\omega}}{B}\Psi_{k}+C_{\nu}.

Here, C†,ω>0C_{\dagger,\omega}>0 is the mean-squared smoothness constant from Lemma B.1, which controls the estimation error induced by policy updates. The additive variance term CνC_{\nu} combines the contributions of full-batch refreshes and recursive mini-batch updates, weighted by pp and α2\alpha^{2}, respectively. From the LL-smoothness of the objective obtained in Proposition 3.1, letting rk≔𝔼⁡[𝒥~∗−𝒥⁡(𝜽k)]r_{k}\coloneqq\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\mathcal{J}}^{*}-\mathcal{J}(\bm{\theta}_{k})], we obtain the recursion of the suboptimality gap:

rk+1≤rk−η8​𝔼​[‖𝒢η​(𝜽k)‖22]+3​η4​Δk−(14​η−L2)​Ψk.\displaystyle r_{k+1}\leq r_{k}-\frac{\eta}{8}\mathbb{E}\left[\|\mathcal{G}_{\eta}(\bm{\theta}_{k})\|_{2}^{2}\right]+\frac{3\eta}{4}\Delta_{k}-\left(\frac{1}{4\eta}-\frac{L}{2}\right)\Psi_{k}.

To establish convergence, we study the potential Φk≔rk+c​Δk\Phi_{k}\coloneqq r_{k}+c\Delta_{k}, combining suboptimality and estimation error. Choosing c=3​η2​λc=\frac{3\eta}{2\lambda} and a sufficiently small step size η\eta yields a recursion in which both objective improvement and estimator-error decay contribute to reducing Φk\Phi_{k}.

Part II: WGD and Recurrence. Because ‖𝒢η​(𝜽k)‖22\|\mathcal{G}_{\eta}(\bm{\theta}_{k})\|_{2}^{2} provides only local stationarity guarantees, we use Assumption 3.2 to bound the global suboptimality gap directly by the gradient mapping norm. Evaluating the invariant sequence xk≔max⁡{0,Φk}x_{k}\coloneqq\max\{0,\Phi_{k}\} reveals a dual-regime dynamical system:

xk+1≤xk−min⁡{μ​η32​xk2,λ4​xk}+3​η​Cν2​λ.\displaystyle x_{k+1}\leq x_{k}-\min\left\{\frac{\mu\eta}{32}x_{k}^{2},\frac{\lambda}{4}x_{k}\right\}+\frac{3\eta C_{\nu}}{2\lambda}.

This recurrence yields linear contraction for large values of the Lyapunov potential and a WGD-induced quadratic decrease for smaller values. The additive term 3​η​Cν/(2​λ)3\eta C_{\nu}/(2\lambda) accounts for stochastic gradient-estimation error. When the additive term is sufficiently small, Lemma H.2 bounds the iterations required to reach and remain within the target accuracy:

K≥⌈max⁡{32μ​η​ϵ,4λ}​log⁡(2​Φ0ϵ)⌉.\displaystyle K\geq\left\lceil\max\left\{\frac{32}{\mu\eta\epsilon},\frac{4}{\lambda}\right\}\log\left(\frac{2\Phi_{0}}{\epsilon}\right)\right\rceil.

Part III: Selection of α,p\alpha,p and η\eta. We now choose the hyperparameters to satisfy the accuracy condition Cν=𝒪⁡(μ​λ​ϵ2)C_{\nu}=\mathcal{O}(\mu\lambda\epsilon^{2}) while controlling the sample cost. Setting N=Θ⁡(ϵ−2)N=\Theta(\epsilon^{-2}) and p=𝒪⁡(B​ϵ2)p=\mathcal{O}(B\epsilon^{2}) keeps the expected cost of full-batch refreshes comparable to that of mini-batch updates. Choosing α=𝒪⁡(B​ϵ2)\alpha=\mathcal{O}(B\epsilon^{2}) controls the momentum-dependent contribution to CνC_{\nu}, while requiring p+α=Ω⁡(B​ϵ2)p+\alpha=\Omega(B\epsilon^{2}) ensures sufficient estimator-error decay through λ=Ω⁡(B​ϵ2)\lambda=\Omega(B\epsilon^{2}). With a suitable step size η=Θ⁡(B​ϵ)\eta=\Theta(B\epsilon), these choices yield K=𝒪~​((B​ϵ2)−1)K=\tilde{\mathcal{O}}((B\epsilon^{2})^{-1}) iterations and a total sample complexity n=𝒪~​(ϵ−2)n=\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-2}). ∎

Theorem 5.1 establishes that LVR-PG attains the minimax-optimal sample complexity in the learning framework described in Section 3, up to logarithmic factors and horizon terms, using exclusively first-order updates. Notably, this rate is achieved using a fixed step size η=Θ⁡(B​ϵ)\eta=\Theta(B\epsilon), and the convergence guarantee applies directly to the last-iterate parameter 𝜽K\bm{\theta}_{K}, bypassing the need for trajectory averaging or random iterate selection commonly required in previous works (Liu et al., 2020; Ding et al., 2022). Furthermore, the analysis identifies a continuous two-dimensional region of hyperparameter configurations (p,α)(p,\alpha) for which the nearly optimal sample complexity is guaranteed. As illustrated in Figure 1, the conditions p=𝒪⁡(B​ϵ2)p=\mathcal{O}(B\epsilon^{2}), α=𝒪⁡(B​ϵ2)\alpha=\mathcal{O}(B\epsilon^{2}), and p+α=Ω⁡(B​ϵ2)p+\alpha=\Omega(B\epsilon^{2}), together with the batch-size and learning-rate choices established in the proof, provide sufficient conditions for this guarantee.

Remark 5.1 (Unification of Existing Algorithms).

Existing variance-reduced estimators emerge as boundary limits of this optimal space: setting α=0\alpha=0 or p=0p=0 recovers DEF-PAGE-PG and DEF-STORM-PG, respectively, both strictly preserving the 𝒪~​(ϵ−2)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-2}) sample complexity. Setting p=1p=1 forces full-batch evaluations at every step, recovering vanilla GPOMDP. This choice violates the computational boundary p=𝒪⁡(B​ϵ2)p=\mathcal{O}(B\epsilon^{2}), shifting the algorithm outside the optimal manifold and correctly degrading its complexity to the standard 𝒪~​(ϵ−3)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-3}) rate (Montenegro et al., 2024).

5.1 On Fisher-Non-Degeneracy

We specialize Theorem 5.1 to Fisher-Non-Degenerate (FND) policies in the unconstrained setting Θ=ℝdΘ\Theta=\mathbb{R}^{d_{\Theta}}. This setting allows us to apply the ordinary-gradient domination inequality induced by FND under suitable approximation and concentrability assumptions (Liu et al., 2020; Ding et al., 2022; Fatkhullin et al., 2023), since 𝒢η​(𝜽)=∇𝜽J​(𝜽)\mathcal{G}_{\eta}(\bm{\theta})=\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}). Although FND can also be imposed on constrained parameter sets, projection can remove gradient components, so the gradient bound does not imply the mapping-based WGD condition required by Assumption 3.2.

In the unconstrained setting Θ=ℝdΘ\Theta=\mathbb{R}^{d_{\Theta}}, when the FIM induced by π𝜽\pi_{\bm{\theta}} is uniformly non-degenerate, i.e., 𝑭(𝜽)=𝔼π𝜽[∇𝜽logπ𝜽(∣𝒔)∇𝜽logπ𝜽(∣𝒔)⊤]⪰μF𝑰\bm{F}(\bm{\theta})=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}[\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mid\bm{s})\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mid\bm{s})^{\top}]\succeq\mu_{F}\bm{I} for some μF>0\mu_{F}>0 and every 𝜽∈Θ\bm{\theta}\in\Theta, WGD follows provided that the compatible function approximation error (Agarwal et al., 2021) is bounded. This condition requires 𝔼π𝜽[(Aπ𝜽(𝒔,)−(1−γ)𝒘⊤∇𝜽logπ𝜽(∣𝒔))2]≤ϵbias\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}[(A^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}(\bm{s},)-(1-\gamma)\bm{w}^{\top}\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mid\bm{s}))^{2}]\leq\epsilon_{\text{bias}}, where 𝒘=𝑭​(𝜽)−1​∇𝜽J​(𝜽)\bm{w}=\bm{F}(\bm{\theta})^{-1}\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}) and Aπ𝜽A^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}} is the advantage function of the policy π𝜽\pi_{\bm{\theta}}. Under these conditions, WGD holds with χ=C1/μF\chi=C_{1}/\mu_{F} and ψ=ϵbias​κ/(1−γ)\psi=\sqrt{\epsilon_{\text{bias}}}\kappa/(1-\gamma). Here, κ=sup𝜽∈ℝdΘ‖νπ∗/νπ𝜽‖∞\kappa=\sup_{\bm{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\Theta}}}\|\nu^{\pi^{*}}/\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}\|_{\infty} is a concentrability coefficient, and νπ𝜽\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}} denotes the state-action distribution induced by π𝜽\pi_{\bm{\theta}}. Note that, differently from previous works (Ding et al., 2022; Fatkhullin et al., 2023), we define the expected compatible function approximation error with respect to the current state-action distribution νπ𝜽\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}} rather than the optimal distribution νπ∗\nu^{\pi^{*}}. Bounding the error under νπ∗\nu^{\pi^{*}} is unverifiable because the optimal policy is unknown a priori. Conversely, evaluating this error under νπ𝜽\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}} requires the parametrization to be expressive along the realized optimization trajectory, a verifiable formulation that inherently incurs the statistical penalty κ\kappa within the irreducible bias.

Corollary 5.1 (Sample complexity under FND).

In the unconstrained setting where Θ=ℝdΘ\Theta=\mathbb{R}^{d_{\Theta}}, letting χ=C1/μF\chi=C_{1}/\mu_{F} and ψ=ϵbias​κ/(1−γ)\psi=\sqrt{\epsilon_{\text{bias}}}\kappa/(1-\gamma), assuming κ<∞\kappa<\infty, LVR-PG achieves a suboptimality gap J∗−𝔼⁡[J⁡(𝛉K)]≤ϵbias​κ1−γ+ϵJ^{*}-\mathbb{E}[J(\bm{\theta}_{K})]\leq\frac{\sqrt{\epsilon_{\text{bias}}}\kappa}{1-\gamma}+\epsilon with a total sample complexity of:

n=𝒪~​(Rmax2​C13(1−γ)4​μF3​ϵ2).\displaystyle n=\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\frac{R_{\max}^{2}C_{1}^{3}}{(1-\gamma)^{4}\mu_{F}^{3}\epsilon^{2}}\right).

Corollary 5.1 confirms that when policies satisfy FND, the minimax optimal sample complexity established by Theorem 5.1 is robustly preserved without degradation. We refer the reader to Appendix C for a detailed discussion.

6 Experimental Results

To evaluate the empirical sample efficiency of our framework, we consider CartPole-v1 and Swimmer-v4, covering classic control and MuJoCo locomotion tasks Todorov et al. (2012). The comparisons, hyperparameter ablations, and grid search reported in Appendix I motivate selecting the STORM gradient estimator as the primary representative of LVR-PG, given its better sample efficiency. This configuration uses momentum-based recursive gradient estimates with defensive IS and no full-batch refreshes (p=0p=0, α>0\alpha>0). Figure 2 also includes DEF-PAGE-PG for completeness, showing its lower sample efficiency in the tested settings. Hybrid configurations are examined in Appendix I. We compare DEF-STORM-PG with GPOMDP, which uses fresh on-policy gradient estimates, and N-PG-IGT, which combines normalized updates with implicit gradient transport without importance sampling. These comparisons assess whether recursive variance reduction with defensive IS improves empirical sample efficiency relative to the two baselines. Across both environments, DEF-STORM-PG reaches high returns with fewer trajectories than GPOMDP and DEF-PAGE-PG. On CartPole-v1 DEF-STORM-PG exhibits fewer oscillations than N-PG-IGT, while in Swimmer-v4, the latter converges quickly to a local optimum.

7 Conclusions

We established that purely first-order PG methods can achieve minimax-optimal sample complexity up to logarithmic factors and horizon terms, with minimal assumptions and without second-order assumptions. Our findings suggest several directions for future research. First, the defensive IS mechanism requires evaluating trajectories under a mixture distribution, which inherently requires storing both the current and previous policy parameters. Developing variance-reduction mechanisms that avoid this explicit double sampling would significantly reduce memory overhead. Second, extending the LVR-PG theoretical framework to encompass adaptive gradient methods would bridge the gap between our convergence guarantees and the practical optimization dynamics prevalent in deep RL.

AI use statement

In this work, we used generative AI tools for text polishing, proof assistance, and code generation. We have not used generative AI tools to generate research ideas or to conduct the literature review, and generating figures or data synthesis is not applicable to this work. Additionally, we used generative AI tools to correct grammar and improve readability. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work. Specifically, the core ideas and initial proofs were developed manually by the authors, and AI was subsequently used to polish the presentation of the mathematical proofs. All AI-assisted proofs were checked line by line, and the authors thoroughly reviewed and tested any AI-assisted code for correctness. Appendix A Loopless Variance-Reduced Policy Gradient (LVR-PG)

Algorithm 3 details the interaction protocol used to evaluate the policies. To ensure that the gradient estimates remain unbiased with respect to the infinite-horizon objective without introducing arbitrary truncation, the algorithm relies on a randomized geometric stopping rule. At each time step, the agent samples an action, observes the corresponding reward and state transition, and terminates the episode with probability 1−γ1-\gamma. This guarantees that the trajectory length follows a geometric distribution with expectation (1−γ)−1(1-\gamma)^{-1}.

Algorithm 2 outlines the generic LVR-PG template, which tracks and updates a recursive gradient estimator ∇^𝜽†​J​(𝜽k)\widehat{\nabla}_{\bm{\theta}}^{\dagger}J(\bm{\theta}_{k}) at each iteration kk. The mechanism allowing for switching between full-batch and mini-batch updates relies on a Bernoulli random variable ck∼ℬ⁡(p)c_{k}\sim\mathcal{B}(p) that dictates the estimator’s update rule. When ck=1c_{k}=1, the historical variance is discarded, and the estimator undergoes a full-batch refresh using NN trajectories. Conversely, when ck=0c_{k}=0, the algorithm computes a variance-reduced update using a smaller mini-batch of BB trajectories, modulated by a momentum decay parameter α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1] and an importance sampling operator ω\omega. By specifically choosing the hyperparameters (p,α,ξ)(p,\alpha,\xi), we can instantiate multiple variance-reduced PG algorithms, as summarized in Table 2.

By selecting these parameters, the framework dynamically shifts its algorithmic behavior. PAGE-PG eliminates the recursive momentum term (α=0\alpha=0), relying entirely on the probabilistic refresh rate pp to bound the accumulation of estimation error alongside standard importance sampling Gargiani et al. (2022). STORM-PG avoids full-batch refreshes entirely (p=0p=0) and instead uses a momentum parameter α\alpha to incrementally discount past gradient errors Yuan et al. (2020).

Crucially, the parameter ξ∈(0,1)\xi\in(0,1) activates the defensive importance sampling mechanism. As detailed in the recursive branch of Algorithm 2, drawing the Bernoulli mixture variable u∼ℬ⁡(ξ)u\sim\mathcal{B}(\xi) physically constructs the defensive trajectory distribution qξ​(τ)=ξ​p𝜽k+1​(τ)+(1−ξ)​p𝜽k​(τ)q_{\xi}(\tau)=\xi p_{\bm{\theta}_{k+1}}(\tau)+(1-\xi)p_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}(\tau). Under this regime, the IS operator ω⁡(𝜽,τ)\omega(\bm{\theta},\tau) evaluates precisely to the density ratio p𝜽​(τ)/qξ​(τ)p_{\bm{\theta}}(\tau)/q_{\xi}(\tau), intrinsically bounding the variance of the off-policy estimator without requiring arbitrary structural constraints on the policy class. While the generic LVR-PG template accommodates standard importance sampling (ξ=0\xi=0), throughout the theoretical analysis and empirical evaluations of this paper, we strictly consider the defensive setting (ξ∈(0,1)\xi\in(0,1)).

We utilize the LVR-PG framework to unify the theoretical analysis of these diverse algorithms. By defining an effective decay rate λ≔1−(1−p)​(1−α)2\lambda\coloneqq 1-(1-p)(1-\alpha)^{2}, we encapsulate the error discounting effects of both probabilistic refreshes and continuous momentum into the exact same mathematical recurrence. This unified rate establishes the variance bound evaluated in Lemma D.4, allowing us to prove last-iterate global convergence in Theorem 5.1.

Appendix B Mean-Squared Smoothness

Because algorithms recursively update their gradient estimators using historical information, they must evaluate the difference between stochastic gradients at the current policy 𝜽k\bm{\theta}_{k} and a previous policy 𝜽k−1\bm{\theta}_{k-1} using a shared batch of trajectories. To correct for the shift in the trajectory distribution, these methods evaluate the gradients using an importance sampling (IS) operator ω\omega. The mean-squared smoothness isolates the expected squared error of this gradient difference, taking the generic form:

𝔼τ​[‖ω⁡(𝜽k,τ)​𝒈​(τ∣𝜽k)−ω⁡(𝜽k−1,τ)​𝒈​(τ∣𝜽k−1)‖22]≤C†,ω​‖𝜽k−𝜽k−1‖22,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\tau}\left[\left\|\omega(\bm{\theta}_{k},\tau)\bm{g}(\tau\mid\bm{\theta}_{k})-\omega(\bm{\theta}_{k-1},\tau)\bm{g}(\tau\mid\bm{\theta}_{k-1})\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]\leq C_{\dagger,\omega}\|\bm{\theta}_{k}-\bm{\theta}_{k-1}\|_{2}^{2}, (3)

where C†,ω>0C_{\dagger,\omega}>0 is a unified bounding constant. In the following, we provide the mean-squared smoothness constants for different instantiations of Algorithm 2.

To avoid the unrealistic assumption of bounded variance for standard importance weights, which is frequently violated in continuous policy spaces, our framework relies entirely on defensive importance sampling (Owen and Zhou, 2000; Paczolay et al., 2024). Consequently, we evaluate the mean-squared smoothness strictly under the defensive mixture distribution qξq_{\xi}, which intrinsically bounds the variance without requiring arbitrary structural constraints.

Lemma B.1 (Mean-Squared Smoothness for LVR-PG).

For the LVR-PG framework, sampling from a defensive mixture distribution qξ​(τ)=ξ​p𝛉k​(τ)+(1−ξ)​p𝛉k−1​(τ)q_{\xi}(\tau)=\xi p_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}(\tau)+(1-\xi)p_{\bm{\theta}_{k-1}}(\tau) with parameter ξ∈(0,1)\xi\in(0,1), the unified mean-squared smoothness constant CDEF,ωC_{\texttt{DEF},\omega} is strictly bounded. Letting mξ≔min⁡{ξ,1−ξ}m_{\xi}\coloneqq\min\{\xi,1-\xi\} and Mr≔𝔼⁡[Hγr]M_{r}\coloneqq\mathbb{E}[H_{\gamma}^{r}] denote the moments of the geometrically distributed trajectory length, under Assumption 3.1 and bounded rewards, it holds that:

𝔼τ∼qξ​[‖ω⁡(𝜽k,τ)​𝒈​(τ∣𝜽k)−ω⁡(𝜽k−1,τ)​𝒈​(τ∣𝜽k−1)‖22]≤C†,ω​‖𝜽k−𝜽k−1‖22,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim q_{\xi}}\left[\left\|\omega(\bm{\theta}_{k},\tau)\bm{g}(\tau\mid\bm{\theta}_{k})-\omega(\bm{\theta}_{k-1},\tau)\bm{g}(\tau\mid\bm{\theta}_{k-1})\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]\leq C_{\dagger,\omega}\|\bm{\theta}_{k}-\bm{\theta}_{k-1}\|_{2}^{2},

where the unified mean-squared smoothness constant is:

C†,ω=Rmax2mξ​(C14​M5+2​LS2​M4).\displaystyle C_{\dagger,\omega}=\frac{R_{\max}^{2}}{m_{\xi}}\left(C_{1}^{4}M_{5}+2L_{S}^{2}M_{4}\right).

Setting ξ=1/2\xi=1/2 minimizes the variance bound, yielding m1/2=1/2m_{1/2}=1/2 and the optimized mean-squared smoothness constant for both algorithms:

C†,ω=2​Rmax2​(C14​M5+2​LS2​M4)=𝒪⁡((1−γ)−5).\displaystyle C_{\dagger,\omega}=2R_{\max}^{2}\left(C_{1}^{4}M_{5}+2L_{S}^{2}M_{4}\right)=\mathcal{O}\left((1-\gamma)^{-5}\right).
Proof.

We recall a result by Paczolay et al. (2024), proved here for completeness. To establish the mean-squared smoothness bound for both algorithms, we must bound the expected squared L2L_{2} norm of the difference between the defensive gradient estimators evaluated at consecutive iterates 𝜽k\bm{\theta}_{k} and 𝜽k−1\bm{\theta}_{k-1}. For brevity, we drop the trajectory dependency and denote p𝜽k=p𝜽k​(τ)p_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}=p_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}(\tau), 𝒈k=𝒈⁡(τ∣𝜽k)\bm{g}_{k}=\bm{g}(\tau\mid\bm{\theta}_{k}), and ω𝜽k=p𝜽kqξ\omega_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}=\frac{p_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}}{q_{\xi}}. We decouple the gradient difference algebraically by adding and subtracting ω𝜽k−1​𝒈k\omega_{\bm{\theta}_{k-1}}\bm{g}_{k}:

ω𝜽k​𝒈k−ω𝜽k−1​𝒈k−1=(ω𝜽k−ω𝜽k−1)​𝒈k+ω𝜽k−1​(𝒈k−𝒈k−1).\displaystyle\omega_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}\bm{g}_{k}-\omega_{\bm{\theta}_{k-1}}\bm{g}_{k-1}=(\omega_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}-\omega_{\bm{\theta}_{k-1}})\bm{g}_{k}+\omega_{\bm{\theta}_{k-1}}(\bm{g}_{k}-\bm{g}_{k-1}).

Applying the inequality ‖x+y‖22≤2​‖x‖22+2​‖y‖22\|x+y\|_{2}^{2}\leq 2\|x\|_{2}^{2}+2\|y\|_{2}^{2}, we can bound the expectation by isolating the importance weights from the on-policy gradients:

𝔼τ∼qξ​[‖ω𝜽k​𝒈k−ω𝜽k−1​𝒈k−1‖22]≤2​𝔼τ∼qξ​[‖(ω𝜽k−ω𝜽k−1)​𝒈k‖22]+2​𝔼τ∼qξ​[‖ω𝜽k−1​(𝒈k−𝒈k−1)‖22].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim q_{\xi}}\left[\left\|\omega_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}\bm{g}_{k}-\omega_{\bm{\theta}_{k-1}}\bm{g}_{k-1}\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]\leq 2\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim q_{\xi}}\left[\left\|(\omega_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}-\omega_{\bm{\theta}_{k-1}})\bm{g}_{k}\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]+2\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim q_{\xi}}\left[\left\|\omega_{\bm{\theta}_{k-1}}(\bm{g}_{k}-\bm{g}_{k-1})\right\|_{2}^{2}\right].

We evaluate the two terms independently. For the first term, we substitute ω𝜽k−ω𝜽k−1=p𝜽k−p𝜽k−1qξ\omega_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}-\omega_{\bm{\theta}_{k-1}}=\frac{p_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}-p_{\bm{\theta}_{k-1}}}{q_{\xi}} and use the definition of the defensive mixture qξ​(τ)≥mξ​(p𝜽k​(τ)+p𝜽k−1​(τ))q_{\xi}(\tau)\geq m_{\xi}(p_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}(\tau)+p_{\bm{\theta}_{k-1}}(\tau)) to bound the density ratio:

(p𝜽k−p𝜽k−1)2qξ≤1mξ​(p𝜽k−p𝜽k−1)2p𝜽k+p𝜽k−1=1mξ​(p𝜽k−p𝜽k−1)2​(p𝜽k+p𝜽k−1)2p𝜽k+p𝜽k−1≤2mξ​(p𝜽k−p𝜽k−1)2.\displaystyle\frac{(p_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}-p_{\bm{\theta}_{k-1}})^{2}}{q_{\xi}}\leq\frac{1}{m_{\xi}}\frac{(p_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}-p_{\bm{\theta}_{k-1}})^{2}}{p_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}+p_{\bm{\theta}_{k-1}}}=\frac{1}{m_{\xi}}(\sqrt{p_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}}-\sqrt{p_{\bm{\theta}_{k-1}}})^{2}\frac{(\sqrt{p_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}}+\sqrt{p_{\bm{\theta}_{k-1}}})^{2}}{p_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}+p_{\bm{\theta}_{k-1}}}\leq\frac{2}{m_{\xi}}(\sqrt{p_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}}-\sqrt{p_{\bm{\theta}_{k-1}}})^{2}.

By bounded rewards and Assumption 3.1, the pathwise GPOMDP gradient is bounded by ‖𝒈k‖2≤Rmax​C1​Hγ2\|\bm{g}_{k}\|_{2}\leq R_{\max}C_{1}H_{\gamma}^{2}. Expanding the expectation of the first term yields:

𝔼τ∼qξ​[‖(ω𝜽k−ω𝜽k−1)​𝒈k‖22]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim q_{\xi}}\left[\left\|(\omega_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}-\omega_{\bm{\theta}_{k-1}})\bm{g}_{k}\right\|_{2}^{2}\right] =∫(p𝜽k−p𝜽k−1)2qξ​‖𝒈k‖22​𝑑τ\displaystyle=\int\frac{(p_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}-p_{\bm{\theta}_{k-1}})^{2}}{q_{\xi}}\|\bm{g}_{k}\|_{2}^{2}d\tau
≤2​Rmax2​C12mξ​∫Hγ4​(p𝜽k−p𝜽k−1)2​𝑑τ.\displaystyle\leq\frac{2R_{\max}^{2}C_{1}^{2}}{m_{\xi}}\int H_{\gamma}^{4}(\sqrt{p_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}}-\sqrt{p_{\bm{\theta}_{k-1}}})^{2}d\tau.

Applying Lemma D.3 with r=4r=4 we obtain:

𝔼τ∼qξ​[‖(ω𝜽k−ω𝜽k−1)​𝒈k‖22]≤Rmax2​C14​M52​mξ​‖𝜽k−𝜽k−1‖22.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim q_{\xi}}\left[\left\|(\omega_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}-\omega_{\bm{\theta}_{k-1}})\bm{g}_{k}\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]\leq\frac{R_{\max}^{2}C_{1}^{4}M_{5}}{2m_{\xi}}\|\bm{\theta}_{k}-\bm{\theta}_{k-1}\|_{2}^{2}.

For the second term, we use the property qξ≥(1−ξ)​p𝜽k−1≥mξ​p𝜽k−1q_{\xi}\geq(1-\xi)p_{\bm{\theta}_{k-1}}\geq m_{\xi}p_{\bm{\theta}_{k-1}} to convert the expectation under the defensive mixture back to the behavior policy distribution:

𝔼τ∼qξ​[‖ω𝜽k−1​(𝒈k−𝒈k−1)‖22]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim q_{\xi}}\left[\|\omega_{\bm{\theta}_{k-1}}(\bm{g}_{k}-\bm{g}_{k-1})\|_{2}^{2}\right] =∫p𝜽k−12qξ​‖𝒈k−𝒈k−1‖22​𝑑τ\displaystyle=\int\frac{p_{\bm{\theta}_{k-1}}^{2}}{q_{\xi}}\|\bm{g}_{k}-\bm{g}_{k-1}\|_{2}^{2}d\tau
≤1mξ​𝔼τ∼p𝜽k−1​[‖𝒈k−𝒈k−1‖22].\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{m_{\xi}}\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p_{\bm{\theta}_{k-1}}}\left[\|\bm{g}_{k}-\bm{g}_{k-1}\|_{2}^{2}\right].

Applying the mean-square continuity of the policy scores (Assumption 3.1) and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality over the sequence of rewards, the expected squared difference of the gradients is bounded by:

=Rmax2mξ​(C14​M5+2​LS2​M4)​‖𝜽k−𝜽k−1‖22.\displaystyle=\frac{R_{\max}^{2}}{m_{\xi}}\left(C_{1}^{4}M_{5}+2L_{S}^{2}M_{4}\right)\|\bm{\theta}_{k}-\bm{\theta}_{k-1}\|_{2}^{2}.

∎

DEF-PAGE-PG, DEF-STORM-PG (CDEF,ωC_{\texttt{DEF},\omega}).

Although DEF-PAGE-PG and DEF-STORM-PG employ different outer recursive mechanisms, their consecutive estimation bounds are identical. This equivalence arises because both algorithms utilize the exact same GPOMDP gradient estimator and rely on the defensive mixture distribution qξ​(τ)=ξ​p𝜽k​(τ)+(1−ξ)​p𝜽k−1​(τ)q_{\xi}(\tau)=\xi p_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}(\tau)+(1-\xi)p_{\bm{\theta}_{k-1}}(\tau) to control the variance of the importance weights. Since the mean squared smoothness isolates only the expected squared error between gradient estimates at consecutive policies, it is strictly independent of the outer update rule. We can verify this by algebraically splitting the update in the recursive branch of Algorithm 2:

∇^𝜽†​J​(𝜽k+1)\displaystyle\widehat{\nabla}^{\dagger}_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k+1}) =(1−α)​1B​∑i=1Bω⁡(𝜽k+1,τi)​𝒈​(τi∣𝜽k+1)+α​1B​∑i=1Bω⁡(𝜽k+1,τi)​𝒈​(τi∣𝜽k+1)\displaystyle=(1-\alpha)\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\omega(\bm{\theta}_{k+1},\tau_{i})\bm{g}(\tau_{i}\mid\bm{\theta}_{k+1})+\alpha\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\omega(\bm{\theta}_{k+1},\tau_{i})\bm{g}(\tau_{i}\mid\bm{\theta}_{k+1})
+(1−α)​[∇^𝜽†​J​(𝜽k)−1B​∑i=1Bω⁡(𝜽k,τi)​𝒈​(τi∣𝜽k)].\displaystyle\quad+(1-\alpha)\left[\widehat{\nabla}^{\dagger}_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k})-\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\omega(\bm{\theta}_{k},\tau_{i})\bm{g}(\tau_{i}\mid\bm{\theta}_{k})\right].

Substituting this back into the update rule allows us to group the gradient difference directly:

∇^𝜽†​J​(𝜽k+1)\displaystyle\widehat{\nabla}^{\dagger}_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k+1}) =(1−α)​∇^𝜽†​J​(𝜽k)+(1−α)​[1B​∑i=1B(ω⁡(𝜽k+1,τi)​𝒈​(τi∣𝜽k+1)−ω⁡(𝜽k,τi)​𝒈​(τi∣𝜽k))]\displaystyle=(1-\alpha)\widehat{\nabla}^{\dagger}_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k})+(1-\alpha)\left[\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\left(\omega(\bm{\theta}_{k+1},\tau_{i})\bm{g}(\tau_{i}\mid\bm{\theta}_{k+1})-\omega(\bm{\theta}_{k},\tau_{i})\bm{g}(\tau_{i}\mid\bm{\theta}_{k})\right)\right]
+α1B∑i=1Bω(𝜽k+1,τi)𝒈(τi∣𝜽k+1).\displaystyle\quad+\alpha\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\omega(\bm{\theta}_{k+1},\tau_{i})\bm{g}(\tau_{i}\mid\bm{\theta}_{k+1}).

Hence, adding the continuous momentum does not alter the underlying variance of the defensive gradient differences. By exploiting the mean-square continuity of the scores (Assumption 3.1), defensive importance sampling strictly bounds the mean-squared smoothness without relying on unbounded uniform assumptions or arbitrary Hessian limits.

Appendix C On Fisher-non-Degeneracy

Assumption C.1 (Fisher-non-degeneracy).

There exists some constant μF>0\mu_{F}>0, such that for every 𝛉∈ℝd\bm{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, the FIM F⁡(θ)F(\theta) induced by the policy π𝛉\pi_{\bm{\theta}} satisfies:

F(𝜽)=𝔼(𝒔,)∼νπ𝜽[∇𝜽logπ𝜽(∣𝒔)∇𝜽logπ𝜽(∣𝒔)⊤]⪰μF⋅𝑰.\displaystyle F(\bm{\theta})=\mathbb{E}_{(\bm{s},)\sim\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}}\left[\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mid\bm{s})\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mid\bm{s})^{\top}\right]\succeq\mu_{F}\cdot\bm{I}. (4)

Assumption C.1 requires the FIM to be uniformly lower-bounded by a strictly positive constant μF>0\mu_{F}>0. This means that the FIM acts as a well-behaved preconditioner in the natural PG update (Kakade, 2001; Ding et al., 2022) Geometrically, the FIM characterizes the local curvature of the policy manifold measured via the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence. This condition mathematically implies that the parameterization contains no redundant or ”flat” directions: any non-zero update in the parameter space 𝜽\bm{\theta} must induce a strictly positive change in the statistical behavior of the policy.

The validity of the FND assumption fundamentally depends on the chosen policy architecture and the underlying feature representation.

Gaussian Policies.

In continuous action spaces, consider a Gaussian policy with a linearly parameterized mean and a fixed covariance matrix, π𝜽​(a∣s)=𝒩⁡(ϕ​(𝒔)⊤​𝜽,Σ)\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(a\mid s)=\mathcal{N}(\phi(\bm{s})^{\top}\bm{\theta},\Sigma). The FIM is proportional to the uncentered covariance of the state features: F⁡(𝜽)=𝔼νπ𝜽​[ϕ⁡(s)​Σ−1​ϕ​(s)⊤]F(\bm{\theta})=\mathbb{E}_{\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}}[\phi(s)\Sigma^{-1}\phi(s)^{\top}]. Here, FND holds globally if and only if the feature covariance matrix is strictly positive definite. This requires the basis functions ϕ⁡(s)\phi(s) to be linearly independent and the state distribution to provide sufficiently rich coverage. When the mean of the gaussian policy μ𝜽​(𝒔)\mu_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{s}) is nonliner in 𝜽\bm{\theta}, as in the case of (deep) neural networks, Assumption C.1 can be satisfied under assumptions on the Jacobian ∇𝜽μ𝜽​(𝒔)\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\mu_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{s}) similar to the ones for the linear case (Fatkhullin et al., 2023).

Softmax Policies.

For discrete action spaces using a softmax parameterization, the elements of the FIM depend directly on the policy’s action probabilities. If the policy approaches determinism (i.e., π𝜽​(a∣s)→0\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(a\mid s)\to 0 for suboptimal actions), the corresponding entries in the FIM vanish, driving the minimum eigenvalue μF\mu_{F} toward zero (Ding et al., 2022). In this case, strict global FND cannot hold without specific architectural constraints or regularization (Cesani et al., 2026).

The FND setting contains more than (linear) Gaussians: in addition, Assumption C.1 holds for every full-rank exponential parametrization with their mean parametrized with μ𝜽​(𝒔)\mu_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{s}) if μ𝜽​(𝒔)\mu_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{s}) is full rank for all 𝜽∈Θ\bm{\theta}\in\Theta. We refer to Section 8 of Ding et al. (2022) and Appendix B of Fatkhullin et al. (2023) for a detailed discussion of FND.

Assumption C.2 (Compatible Function Approximation Error).

There exist a constant ϵbias>0\epsilon_{\text{bias}}>0, such that for every 𝛉∈ℝd\bm{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, the transferred compatible function approximation error satisfies

𝔼νπ𝜽[(Aπ𝜽(𝒔,)−(1−γ)𝒖∗⁣⊤∇𝜽logπ𝜽(∣𝒔))2]≤ϵbias,\displaystyle\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}}\left[\left(A^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}(\bm{s},)-(1-\gamma)\bm{u}^{*\top}\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mid\bm{s})\right)^{2}\right]\leq\epsilon_{\text{bias}}, (5)

where νπ𝛉\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}} is the state-action distribution induced by a policy π𝛉\pi_{\bm{\theta}} and 𝐮∗≔F​(𝛉)−1​∇𝛉J​(𝛉)\bm{u}^{*}\coloneqq F(\bm{\theta})^{-1}\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}) is the solution of

min𝒘∈ℝd𝔼νπ𝜽[(Aπ𝜽(𝒔,)−(1−γ)𝒘⊤∇𝜽logπ𝜽(∣𝒔))2].\displaystyle\min_{\bm{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}}\left[\left(A^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}(\bm{s},)-(1-\gamma)\bm{w}^{\top}\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mid\bm{s})\right)^{2}\right].

Assumption C.2 bounds the error incurred when approximating the advantage function Aπ𝜽​(s,a)A^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}(s,a) using the score function ∇𝜽logπ𝜽(∣𝒔)\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mid\bm{s}) as a linear feature representation. The vector 𝒖∗≔F​(𝜽)−1​∇𝜽J​(𝜽)\bm{u}^{*}\coloneqq F(\bm{\theta})^{-1}\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}) is exactly the minimizer of this weighted least-squares regression problem. As established by (Agarwal et al., 2021), this assumption characterizes the expressivity of the parameterized policy class. If the policy class is sufficiently rich, e.g., highly parameterized neural networks or softmax tabular policies, this transferred approximation error ϵbias\epsilon_{\text{bias}} is small.

A critical theoretical distinction must be done between Assumption C.2 and analogous assumptions utilized in the recent variance-reduced policy optimization literature. For instance, the analysis of STORM-PG-S by (Ding et al., 2022) requires the compatible function approximation error to be bounded under the state-action distribution of the optimal policy, νπ∗\nu^{\pi^{*}}. In contrast, our formulation strictly evaluates the expectation under the state-action distribution of the current policy, νπ𝜽\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}.

This difference is motivated by the fact that assuming a bounded approximation error under νπ∗\nu^{\pi^{*}} means requiring that the agent has information about the optimal policy, which is not possible. This is because it is not possible to guarantee that the current parametrization accurately fits the advantage function over regions of the state-action space visited by an optimal policy π∗\pi^{*}, which is is entirely unknown. By defining the expectation over νπ𝜽\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}, Assumption C.2 is entirely related to the policy that is being optimized, from which we can gather information about its state-action distribution.

Lemma C.1 (Fisher-induced Gradient Domination).

Let us consider a general Fisher-non-degenerate policy π𝛉\pi_{\bm{\theta}} satisfying Assumptions C.1,  3.1, and C.2 in the unconstrained parameter space Θ=ℝdΘ\Theta=\mathbb{R}^{d_{\Theta}}. Assume additionally that sup𝛉∈Θ‖νπ𝛉∗/ν𝛉π‖∞<∞\sup_{\bm{\theta}\in\Theta}\left\|\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}^{*}}}/\nu^{\pi}_{\bm{\theta}}\right\|_{\infty}<\infty, where the ratio denotes the Radon–Nikodym derivative. Then, we have:

J⁡(𝜽∗)−J⁡(𝜽)≤ϵbias1−γ​‖νπ𝜽∗ν𝜽π‖∞+C1μF​‖∇𝜽J​(𝜽)‖2.\displaystyle J(\bm{\theta}^{*})-J(\bm{\theta})\leq\frac{\sqrt{\epsilon_{\text{bias}}}}{1-\gamma}\left\|\frac{\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}^{*}}}}{\nu^{\pi}_{\bm{\theta}}}\right\|_{\infty}+\frac{C_{1}}{\mu_{F}}\|\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta})\|_{2}.
Proof.

The proof follows the one provided by Ding et al. (2022), with the expectation of Assumption C.2 defined w.r.t. the current policy π𝜽\pi_{\bm{\theta}} instead of the optimal policy π∗\pi^{*}. We begin with the performance-difference lemma and perform a change of distribution:

J⁡(𝜽∗)−J⁡(𝜽)\displaystyle J(\bm{\theta}^{*})-J(\bm{\theta}) =11−γ𝔼(𝒔,)∼νπ∗[Aπ𝜽(𝒔,)]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\mathbb{E}_{(\bm{s},)\sim\nu^{\pi^{*}}}\left[A^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}(\bm{s},)\right]
=11−γ𝔼(𝒔,)∼νπ𝜽[Aπ𝜽(𝒔,)νπ𝜽∗(𝒔,)νπ𝜽(𝒔,)].\displaystyle=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\mathbb{E}_{(\bm{s},)\sim\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}}\left[A^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}(\bm{s},)\frac{\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}^{*}}}(\bm{s},)}{\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}(\bm{s},)}\right].

By introducing the optimal compatible weights u∗:=F​(𝜽)−1​∇𝜽J​(𝜽)u^{*}:=F(\bm{\theta})^{-1}\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}) and adding and subtracting (1−γ)u∗⁣⊤∇𝜽logπ𝜽(∣𝒔)(1-\gamma)u^{*\top}\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mid\bm{s}), we obtain:

J⁡(𝜽∗)−J⁡(𝜽)\displaystyle J(\bm{\theta}^{*})-J(\bm{\theta}) =11−γ𝔼(𝒔,)∼νπ𝜽[(Aπ𝜽(𝒔,)−(1−γ)u∗⁣⊤∇𝜽logπ𝜽(∣𝒔))νπ𝜽∗(𝒔,)νπ𝜽(𝒔,)]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\mathbb{E}_{(\bm{s},)\sim\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}}\left[\left(A^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}(\bm{s},)-(1-\gamma)u^{*\top}\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mid\bm{s})\right)\frac{\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}^{*}}}(\bm{s},)}{\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}(\bm{s},)}\right]
+𝔼(𝒔,)∼νπ𝜽∗[u∗⁣⊤∇𝜽logπ𝜽(∣𝒔)].\displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}_{(\bm{s},)\sim\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}^{*}}}}\left[u^{*\top}\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mid\bm{s})\right].

To bound the right-hand side, we evaluate the two terms independently. Applying Hölder’s inequality to the first term, followed by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, gives:

|𝔼(𝒔,)∼νπ𝜽[(Aπ𝜽(𝒔,)−(1−γ)u∗⁣⊤∇𝜽logπ𝜽(∣𝒔))νπ𝜽∗(𝒔,)νπ𝜽(𝒔,)]|\displaystyle\left|\mathbb{E}_{(\bm{s},)\sim\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}}\left[\left(A^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}(\bm{s},)-(1-\gamma)u^{*\top}\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mid\bm{s})\right)\frac{\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}^{*}}}(\bm{s},)}{\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}(\bm{s},)}\right]\right|
≤‖νπ𝜽∗νπ𝜽‖∞𝔼(𝒔,)∼νπ𝜽[|Aπ𝜽(𝒔,)−(1−γ)u∗⁣⊤∇𝜽logπ𝜽(∣𝒔)|]\displaystyle\qquad\leq\left\|\frac{\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}^{*}}}}{\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}}\right\|_{\infty}\mathbb{E}_{(\bm{s},)\sim\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}}\left[\left|A^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}(\bm{s},)-(1-\gamma)u^{*\top}\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mid\bm{s})\right|\right]
≤‖νπ𝜽∗νπ𝜽‖∞​𝔼(𝒔,)∼νπ𝜽[(Aπ𝜽(𝒔,)−(1−γ)u∗⁣⊤∇𝜽logπ𝜽(∣𝒔))2]\displaystyle\qquad\leq\left\|\frac{\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}^{*}}}}{\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}}\right\|_{\infty}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{(\bm{s},)\sim\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}}\left[\left(A^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}(\bm{s},)-(1-\gamma)u^{*\top}\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mid\bm{s})\right)^{2}\right]}
≤ϵbias​‖νπ𝜽∗νπ𝜽‖∞,\displaystyle\qquad\leq\sqrt{\epsilon_{\text{bias}}}\left\|\frac{\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}^{*}}}}{\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}}\right\|_{\infty},

where the final inequality follows from Assumption C.2. For the second term, the bounded score condition in Assumption 3.1 and Fisher-non-degeneracy give:

𝔼(𝒔,)∼νπ𝜽∗[u∗⁣⊤∇𝜽logπ𝜽(∣𝒔)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{(\bm{s},)\sim\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}^{*}}}}\left[u^{*\top}\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mid\bm{s})\right] ≤∥u∗∥2𝔼(𝒔,)∼νπ𝜽∗[∥∇𝜽logπ𝜽(∣𝒔)∥2]\displaystyle\leq\|u^{*}\|_{2}\mathbb{E}_{(\bm{s},)\sim\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}^{*}}}}\left[\|\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mid\bm{s})\|_{2}\right]
≤C1​‖u∗‖2\displaystyle\leq C_{1}\|u^{*}\|_{2}
=C1​‖F​(𝜽)−1​∇𝜽J​(𝜽)‖2\displaystyle=C_{1}\|F(\bm{\theta})^{-1}\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta})\|_{2}
≤C1μF​‖∇𝜽J​(𝜽)‖2.\displaystyle\leq\frac{C_{1}}{\mu_{F}}\|\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta})\|_{2}.

Combining the two bounds yields:

J⁡(𝜽∗)−J⁡(𝜽)≤ϵbias1−γ​‖νπ𝜽∗νπ𝜽‖∞+C1μF​‖∇𝜽J​(𝜽)‖2.\displaystyle J(\bm{\theta}^{*})-J(\bm{\theta})\leq\frac{\sqrt{\epsilon_{\text{bias}}}}{1-\gamma}\left\|\frac{\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}^{*}}}}{\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}}\right\|_{\infty}+\frac{C_{1}}{\mu_{F}}\|\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta})\|_{2}.

∎

As discussed in Agarwal et al. (2021), analyzing PG methods requires carefully analyzing distinct sources of error: the statistical regression error and the mismatch in state-action visitations. By adopting the formulation in Assumption C.2, the representational capacity of the model is captured entirely by ϵbias\epsilon_{\text{bias}} under the data-generating distribution νπ𝜽\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}. Consequently, the structural penalty for not visiting optimal states is explicitly isolated and paid later in the Fisher-induced Gradient Domination Lemma, manifesting as the concentrability coefficient κ=‖νπ∗νπ𝜽‖∞\kappa=\left\|\frac{\nu^{\pi^{*}}}{\nu^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}}\right\|_{\infty}.

Here, the lemmas used in the proofs of the main results are presented.

Under Assumption 3.1(i), the variance of the on-policy gradient estimator is strictly bounded. For all 𝛉∈Θ\bm{\theta}\in\Theta, it holds that:

𝕍​ar​(g⁡(τ∣𝜽))≤4​Rmax2​C12(1−γ)3≕ν2.\displaystyle\mathbb{V}\text{ar}\left(g(\tau\mid\bm{\theta})\right)\leq\frac{4R_{\max}^{2}C_{1}^{2}}{(1-\gamma)^{3}}\eqqcolon\nu^{2}.

≤(∑t=0H−1rt+12)(∑t=0H−1‖∑h=0t∇𝜽logπ𝜽(h∣𝒔h)‖22).\displaystyle\leq\left(\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}r_{t+1}^{2}\right)\left(\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\left\|\sum_{h=0}^{t}\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(_{h}\mid\bm{s}_{h})\right\|_{2}^{2}\right). (6)
