so lim supϵ↓0‖(A)‖ϵ≤Rmax​(h+1)​LS​‖𝜽−𝜽′‖\limsup_{\epsilon\downarrow 0}\frac{\|(A)\|}{\epsilon}\leq R_{\max}(h+1)L_{S}\|\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}^{\prime}\|.

As for the second term, note that, for ℓ<k≤h\ell<k\leq h,

𝔼τ0:k∼p𝜽uk[∇logπ𝜽u(ℓ∣𝒔ℓ)⊤∇logπ𝜽u(k∣𝒔k)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\tau_{0:k}\sim p_{\bm{\theta}_{u}}^{k}}\left[\nabla\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}_{u}}(_{\ell}\mid\bm{s}_{\ell})^{\top}\nabla\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}_{u}}(_{k}\mid\bm{s}_{k})\right]
=𝔼τ0:k∼p𝜽uk[∇logπ𝜽u(ℓ∣𝒔ℓ)⊤𝔼∼π𝜽u(⋅∣𝒔k)[∇logπ𝜽u(∣𝒔k)]]=0,\displaystyle\qquad=\mathbb{E}_{\tau_{0:k}\sim p_{\bm{\theta}_{u}}^{k}}\left[\nabla\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}_{u}}(_{\ell}\mid\bm{s}_{\ell})^{\top}\mathbb{E}_{\sim\pi_{\bm{\theta}_{u}}(\cdot\mid\bm{s}_{k})}\left[\nabla\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}_{u}}(\mid\bm{s}_{k})\right]\right]=0,

so, by the first assumption on the policy scores:

𝔼τ0:h∼p𝜽uh[∥𝒁h(u)∥2]=∑ℓ=0h𝔼τ0:ℓ∼p𝜽uℓ[∥∇logπ𝜽u(ℓ∣𝒔ℓ)∥2]≤(h+1)C12.\mathbb{E}_{\tau_{0:h}\sim p_{\bm{\theta}_{u}}^{h}}[\|\bm{Z}_{h}(u)\|^{2}]=\sum_{\ell=0}^{h}\mathbb{E}_{\tau_{0:\ell}\sim p_{\bm{\theta}_{u}}^{\ell}}[\|\nabla\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}_{u}}(_{\ell}\mid\bm{s}_{\ell})\|^{2}]\leq(h+1)C_{1}^{2}.

Then:

limϵ↓0(B)ϵ\displaystyle\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow 0}\frac{(B)}{\epsilon} =∫limϵ↓0p𝜽u+ϵh(τ0:h)−p𝜽uh(τ0:h)ϵrh+1𝒁h(u)dτ0:h\displaystyle=\int\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow 0}\frac{p_{\bm{\theta}_{u+\epsilon}}^{h}(\tau_{0:h})-p_{\bm{\theta}_{u}}^{h}(\tau_{0:h})}{\epsilon}r_{h+1}\bm{Z}_{h}(u)\mathrm{d}\tau_{0:h}
=∫∇p𝜽uh(τ0:h)⊤(𝜽−𝜽′)rh+1𝒁h(u)dτ0:h\displaystyle=\int\nabla p_{\bm{\theta}_{u}}^{h}(\tau_{0:h})^{\top}(\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}^{\prime})r_{h+1}\bm{Z}_{h}(u)\mathrm{d}\tau_{0:h}
=𝔼τ0:h∼p𝜽uh[𝒁h(u)𝒁h(u)⊤(𝜽−𝜽′)rh+1],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\tau_{0:h}\sim p_{\bm{\theta}_{u}}^{h}}\left[\bm{Z}_{h}(u)\bm{Z}_{h}(u)^{\top}(\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}^{\prime})r_{h+1}\right],

and

‖limϵ↓0(B)ϵ‖\displaystyle\left\|\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow 0}\frac{(B)}{\epsilon}\right\| ≤Rmax𝔼τ0:h∼p𝜽uh[‖𝒁h(u)‖2]∥𝜽−𝜽′∥\displaystyle\leq R_{\max}\mathbb{E}_{\tau_{0:h}\sim p_{\bm{\theta}_{u}}^{h}}\left[\left\|\bm{Z}_{h}(u)\right\|^{2}\right]\|\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}^{\prime}\|
≤Rmax​(h+1)​C12​‖𝜽−𝜽′‖.\displaystyle\leq R_{\max}(h+1)C_{1}^{2}\|\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}^{\prime}\|.

Now, from Equation (9):

lim supϵ↓0‖𝑮h​(u+ϵ)−𝑮h​(u)‖ϵ\displaystyle\limsup_{\epsilon\downarrow 0}\frac{\left\|\bm{G}_{h}(u+\epsilon)-\bm{G}_{h}(u)\right\|}{\epsilon} ≤lim supϵ↓0‖(A)‖ϵ+lim supϵ↓0‖(B)‖ϵ\displaystyle\leq\limsup_{\epsilon\downarrow 0}\frac{\|(A)\|}{\epsilon}+\limsup_{\epsilon\downarrow 0}\frac{\|(B)\|}{\epsilon}
=lim supϵ↓0‖(A)‖ϵ+‖limϵ↓0(B)ϵ‖\displaystyle=\limsup_{\epsilon\downarrow 0}\frac{\|(A)\|}{\epsilon}+\left\|\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow 0}\frac{(B)}{\epsilon}\right\|
≤Rmax​(h+1)​(LS+C12)​‖𝜽−𝜽′‖.\displaystyle\leq R_{\max}(h+1)(L_{S}+C_{1}^{2})\|\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}^{\prime}\|.

The same decomposition shows that 𝑮h\bm{G}_{h} is continuous on [0,1][0,1]. By Lemma H.1:

‖𝑮h​(1)−𝑮h​(0)‖≤Rmax​(h+1)​(LS+C12)​‖𝜽−𝜽′‖.\|\bm{G}_{h}(1)-\bm{G}_{h}(0)\|\leq R_{\max}(h+1)(L_{S}+C_{1}^{2})\|\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}^{\prime}\|.

Finally:

‖∇J​(𝜽′)−∇J​(𝜽)‖\displaystyle\|\nabla J(\bm{\theta}^{\prime})-\nabla J(\bm{\theta})\| ≤∑h=0∞γh​‖𝑮h​(1)−𝑮h​(0)‖\displaystyle\leq\sum_{h=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{h}\|\bm{G}_{h}(1)-\bm{G}_{h}(0)\|
≤Rmax​(LS+C12)​‖𝜽−𝜽′‖​∑h=0∞γh​(h+1)\displaystyle\leq R_{\max}(L_{S}+C_{1}^{2})\|\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}^{\prime}\|\sum_{h=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{h}(h+1)
=Rmax​(LS+C12)(1−γ)2​‖𝜽−𝜽′‖.\displaystyle=\frac{R_{\max}(L_{S}+C_{1}^{2})}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}\|\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}^{\prime}\|.

∎

Lemma D.3 (Weighted Hellinger continuity).

Suppose that Assumption 3.1(1) holds. For every integer r≥0r\geq 0 and every 𝛉1,𝛉2∈Θ\bm{\theta}_{1},\bm{\theta}_{2}\in\Theta,

∫𝒯Hγ​(τ)r​(p⁡(τ∣𝜽1)−p⁡(τ∣𝜽2))2​𝑑τ≤C12​Mr+14​‖𝜽1−𝜽2‖2.\int_{\mathcal{T}}H_{\gamma}(\tau)^{r}\left(\sqrt{p(\tau\mid\bm{\theta}_{1})}-\sqrt{p(\tau\mid\bm{\theta}_{2})}\right)^{2}\mathrm{d}\tau\leq\frac{C_{1}^{2}M_{r+1}}{4}\left\|\bm{\theta}_{1}-\bm{\theta}_{2}\right\|^{2}.
Proof.

We recall a result by Paczolay et al. (2024), proved here for completeness Let

𝜽t=(1−t)​𝜽2+t​𝜽1,𝚫=𝜽1−𝜽2,t∈[0,1].\bm{\theta}_{t}=(1-t)\bm{\theta}_{2}+t\bm{\theta}_{1},\qquad\bm{\Delta}=\bm{\theta}_{1}-\bm{\theta}_{2},\qquad t\in[0,1].

Convexity of Θ\Theta guarantees that 𝜽t∈Θ\bm{\theta}_{t}\in\Theta. Because the stopping rule and the environment are independent of the policy parameters,

∇logp(τ∣𝜽t)=∑h=0Hγ​(τ)−1∇logπ𝜽t(a∣𝒔h).\nabla\log p(\tau\mid\bm{\theta}_{t})=\sum_{h=0}^{H_{\gamma}(\tau)-1}\nabla\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}_{t}}(_{a}\mid\bm{s}_{h}).

Consequently,

dd​t​p⁡(τ∣𝜽t)=12​p⁡(τ∣𝜽t)​⟨𝚫,∇log⁡p​(τ∣𝜽t)⟩.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\sqrt{p(\tau\mid\bm{\theta}_{t})}=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{p(\tau\mid\bm{\theta}_{t})}\left\langle\bm{\Delta},\nabla\log p(\tau\mid\bm{\theta}_{t})\right\rangle.

By the fundamental theorem of calculus and Cauchy–Schwarz,

(p⁡(τ∣𝜽1)−p⁡(τ∣𝜽2))2\displaystyle\left(\sqrt{p(\tau\mid\bm{\theta}_{1})}-\sqrt{p(\tau\mid\bm{\theta}_{2})}\right)^{2}
≤‖𝚫‖24​∫01p⁡(τ∣𝜽t)​‖∇log⁡p​(τ∣𝜽t)‖2​𝑑t.\displaystyle\qquad\leq\frac{\|\bm{\Delta}\|^{2}}{4}\int_{0}^{1}p(\tau\mid\bm{\theta}_{t})\left\|\nabla\log p(\tau\mid\bm{\theta}_{t})\right\|^{2}\mathrm{d}t.

Multiplying by Hγ​(τ)rH_{\gamma}(\tau)^{r} and integrating over τ\tau yields

∫𝒯Hγ​(τ)r​(p⁡(τ∣𝜽1)−p⁡(τ∣𝜽2))2​𝑑τ\displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{T}}H_{\gamma}(\tau)^{r}\left(\sqrt{p(\tau\mid\bm{\theta}_{1})}-\sqrt{p(\tau\mid\bm{\theta}_{2})}\right)^{2}\mathrm{d}\tau
≤‖𝚫‖24∫01𝔼τ∼p(⋅∣𝜽t)[Hγr‖∑h=0Hγ−1∇logπ𝜽t(a∣𝒔h)‖2]dt.\displaystyle\qquad\leq\frac{\|\bm{\Delta}\|^{2}}{4}\int_{0}^{1}\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p(\cdot\mid\bm{\theta}_{t})}\left[H_{\gamma}^{r}\left\|\sum_{h=0}^{H_{\gamma}-1}\nabla\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}_{t}}(_{a}\mid\bm{s}_{h})\right\|^{2}\right]\mathrm{d}t.

The score increments are martingale differences. Conditionally on HγH_{\gamma}, Assumption 3.1(i) therefore gives

𝔼τ∼p(⋅∣𝜽t)[‖∑h=0Hγ−1∇logπ𝜽t(a∣𝒔h)‖2|Hγ]≤C12Hγ.\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p(\cdot\mid\bm{\theta}_{t})}\left[\left\|\sum_{h=0}^{H_{\gamma}-1}\nabla\log\pi_{\bm{\theta}_{t}}(_{a}\mid\bm{s}_{h})\right\|^{2}\,\middle|\,H_{\gamma}\right]\leq C_{1}^{2}H_{\gamma}.

Since the distribution of HγH_{\gamma} is independent of 𝜽t\bm{\theta}_{t},

𝔼⁡[Hγr​‖∇log⁡p​(τ∣𝜽t)‖2]≤C12​Mr+1.\mathbb{E}\left[H_{\gamma}^{r}\left\|\nabla\log p(\tau\mid\bm{\theta}_{t})\right\|^{2}\right]\leq C_{1}^{2}M_{r+1}.

Substitution proves the claim. ∎

Lemma D.4 (Estimation Error for LVR-PG).

Under Assumption 3.1, let Δk:=𝔼⁡[‖∇^𝛉†​J​(𝛉k)−∇𝛉J​(𝛉k)‖22]\Delta_{k}:=\mathbb{E}[\|\widehat{\nabla}^{\dagger}_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k})-\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k})\|_{2}^{2}] be the estimation error of the LVR-PG estimator. Letting λ≔1−(1−p)​(1−α)2\lambda\coloneqq 1-(1-p)(1-\alpha)^{2} and letting C†,ω>0C_{\dagger,\omega}>0 denote the bound on the variance of the (defensive) importance weights, the following recurrence holds for all k∈⟦K⟧k\in\llbracket K\rrbracket:

Δk+1≤(1−λ)​Δk+2​(1−λ)​C†,ωB​𝔼​[‖𝜽k+1−𝜽k‖22]+Cν,\displaystyle\Delta_{k+1}\leq(1-\lambda)\Delta_{k}+\frac{2(1-\lambda)C_{\dagger,\omega}}{B}\mathbb{E}[\|\bm{\theta}_{k+1}-\bm{\theta}_{k}\|_{2}^{2}]+C_{\nu},

where Cν≔(pN+4​α2​(1−p)B)​ν2C_{\nu}\coloneqq\left(\frac{p}{N}+\frac{4\alpha^{2}(1-p)}{B}\right)\nu^{2}.

Proof.

We analyze the estimation error conditioned on the Bernoulli random variable ck∼ℬ⁡(p)c_{k}\sim\mathcal{B}(p). By the law of total expectation, the expected estimation error Δk+1\Delta_{k+1} decomposes as follows:

Δk+1\displaystyle\Delta_{k+1} =p⋅𝔼⁡[‖∇^𝜽†​J​(𝜽k+1)−∇𝜽J​(𝜽k+1)‖22∣ck=1]\displaystyle=p\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[\|\widehat{\nabla}^{\dagger}_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k+1})-\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k+1})\|_{2}^{2}\mid c_{k}=1\right]
+(1−p)⋅𝔼[∥∇^𝜽†J(𝜽k+1)−∇𝜽J(𝜽k+1)∥22∣ck=0].\displaystyle\quad+(1-p)\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[\|\widehat{\nabla}^{\dagger}_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k+1})-\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k+1})\|_{2}^{2}\mid c_{k}=0\right].

When ck=1c_{k}=1, the estimator executes a full-batch refresh. Because this relies on a new batch of NN on-policy trajectories, the conditional error is bounded by the variance of the standard GPOMDP estimator obtained in Lemma D.1:

𝔼⁡[‖∇^𝜽†​J​(𝜽k+1)−∇𝜽J​(𝜽k+1)‖22∣ck=1]≤ν2N.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\|\widehat{\nabla}^{\dagger}_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k+1})-\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k+1})\|_{2}^{2}\mid c_{k}=1\right]\leq\frac{\nu^{2}}{N}.

When ck=0c_{k}=0, the estimator applies the momentum update. Following the proof of Lemma 8 of Yuan et al. (2020), we condition on the history ℱk\mathcal{F}_{k} available after computing 𝜽k+1\bm{\theta}_{k+1} and before drawing ckc_{k} and the fresh trajectories. Under this conditioning, 𝜽k\bm{\theta}_{k}, 𝜽k+1\bm{\theta}_{k+1}, and ∇^𝜽†​J​(𝜽k)\widehat{\nabla}^{\dagger}_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k}) are fixed, while the fresh trajectories {τi}i=1B\{\tau_{i}\}_{i=1}^{B} are independent samples from ξ​p𝜽k+1+(1−ξ)​p𝜽k\xi p_{\bm{\theta}_{k+1}}+(1-\xi)p_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}. Substituting the momentum update and adding and subtracting the corresponding gradients gives:

∇^𝜽†​J​(𝜽k+1)−∇𝜽J​(𝜽k+1)\displaystyle\widehat{\nabla}^{\dagger}_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k+1})-\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k+1}) =(1−α)​(∇^𝜽†​J​(𝜽k)−∇𝜽J​(𝜽k))\displaystyle=(1-\alpha)(\widehat{\nabla}^{\dagger}_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k})-\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k}))
+(1−α)​[1B​∑i=1B(ωξ​(𝜽k+1,τi)​𝒈​(τi∣𝜽k+1)−ωξ​(𝜽k,τi)​𝒈​(τi∣𝜽k))−∇𝜽J​(𝜽k+1)+∇𝜽J​(𝜽k)]\displaystyle\quad+(1-\alpha)\left[\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\left(\omega_{\xi}(\bm{\theta}_{k+1},\tau_{i})\bm{g}(\tau_{i}\mid\bm{\theta}_{k+1})-\omega_{\xi}(\bm{\theta}_{k},\tau_{i})\bm{g}(\tau_{i}\mid\bm{\theta}_{k})\right)-\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k+1})+\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k})\right]
+α⁡[1B​∑i=1Bωξ​(𝜽k+1,τi)​𝒈​(τi∣𝜽k+1)−∇𝜽J​(𝜽k+1)].\displaystyle\quad+\alpha\left[\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\omega_{\xi}(\bm{\theta}_{k+1},\tau_{i})\bm{g}(\tau_{i}\mid\bm{\theta}_{k+1})-\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k+1})\right].

The three terms represent the previous estimation error, the error in estimating the consecutive-gradient difference, and the current-gradient estimation error, respectively. The latter two have zero conditional expectation by unbiasedness of the weighted estimates. Consequently, their cross terms with the previous estimation error vanish in conditional expectation. Applying ‖u+v‖22≤2​‖u‖22+2​‖v‖22\|u+v\|_{2}^{2}\leq 2\|u\|_{2}^{2}+2\|v\|_{2}^{2} to these two fresh error terms, and using independence across trajectories, yields

𝔼[∥∇^𝜽†J(𝜽k+1)−∇𝜽J(𝜽k+1)∥22∣ℱk,ck=0]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\|\widehat{\nabla}^{\dagger}_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k+1})-\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k+1})\|_{2}^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{k},c_{k}=0\right]
≤(1−α)2​‖∇^𝜽†​J​(𝜽k)−∇𝜽J​(𝜽k)‖22\displaystyle\qquad\leq(1-\alpha)^{2}\|\widehat{\nabla}^{\dagger}_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k})-\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k})\|_{2}^{2}
+2​(1−α)2B​𝔼τ∼ξ​p𝜽k+1+(1−ξ)​p𝜽k​[‖ωξ​(𝜽k+1,τ)​𝒈​(τ∣𝜽k+1)−ωξ​(𝜽k,τ)​𝒈​(τ∣𝜽k)−∇𝜽J​(𝜽k+1)+∇𝜽J​(𝜽k)‖22]\displaystyle\qquad\quad+\frac{2(1-\alpha)^{2}}{B}\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\xi p_{\bm{\theta}_{k+1}}+(1-\xi)p_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}}\left[\left\|\omega_{\xi}(\bm{\theta}_{k+1},\tau)\bm{g}(\tau\mid\bm{\theta}_{k+1})-\omega_{\xi}(\bm{\theta}_{k},\tau)\bm{g}(\tau\mid\bm{\theta}_{k})-\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k+1})+\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k})\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]
+2​α2B​𝔼τ∼ξ​p𝜽k+1+(1−ξ)​p𝜽k​[‖ωξ​(𝜽k+1,τ)​𝒈​(τ∣𝜽k+1)−∇𝜽J​(𝜽k+1)‖22].\displaystyle\qquad\quad+\frac{2\alpha^{2}}{B}\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\xi p_{\bm{\theta}_{k+1}}+(1-\xi)p_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}}\left[\left\|\omega_{\xi}(\bm{\theta}_{k+1},\tau)\bm{g}(\tau\mid\bm{\theta}_{k+1})-\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k+1})\right\|_{2}^{2}\right].

The factors 1/B1/B follow because the centered contributions from distinct trajectories are conditionally independent. For the consecutive-gradient error, removing the centering and applying Lemma B.1 gives

𝔼τ∼ξ​p𝜽k+1+(1−ξ)​p𝜽k​[‖ωξ​(𝜽k+1,τ)​𝒈​(τ∣𝜽k+1)−ωξ​(𝜽k,τ)​𝒈​(τ∣𝜽k)−∇𝜽J​(𝜽k+1)+∇𝜽J​(𝜽k)‖22]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\xi p_{\bm{\theta}_{k+1}}+(1-\xi)p_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}}\left[\left\|\omega_{\xi}(\bm{\theta}_{k+1},\tau)\bm{g}(\tau\mid\bm{\theta}_{k+1})-\omega_{\xi}(\bm{\theta}_{k},\tau)\bm{g}(\tau\mid\bm{\theta}_{k})-\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k+1})+\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k})\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]
≤𝔼τ∼ξ​p𝜽k+1+(1−ξ)​p𝜽k​[‖ωξ​(𝜽k+1,τ)​𝒈​(τ∣𝜽k+1)−ωξ​(𝜽k,τ)​𝒈​(τ∣𝜽k)‖22]\displaystyle\qquad\leq\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\xi p_{\bm{\theta}_{k+1}}+(1-\xi)p_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}}\left[\left\|\omega_{\xi}(\bm{\theta}_{k+1},\tau)\bm{g}(\tau\mid\bm{\theta}_{k+1})-\omega_{\xi}(\bm{\theta}_{k},\tau)\bm{g}(\tau\mid\bm{\theta}_{k})\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]
≤C†,ω​‖𝜽k+1−𝜽k‖22.\displaystyle\qquad\leq C_{\dagger,\omega}\|\bm{\theta}_{k+1}-\bm{\theta}_{k}\|_{2}^{2}.

Here, the first inequality uses the fact that the expectation of the weighted gradient difference is ∇𝜽J​(𝜽k+1)−∇𝜽J​(𝜽k)\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k+1})-\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k}). The second inequality is the mean-squared error bound provided by Lemma B.1. For the current-gradient error, we similarly obtain:

𝔼τ∼ξ​p𝜽k+1+(1−ξ)​p𝜽k​[‖ωξ​(𝜽k+1,τ)​𝒈​(τ∣𝜽k+1)−∇𝜽J​(𝜽k+1)‖22]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\xi p_{\bm{\theta}_{k+1}}+(1-\xi)p_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}}\left[\left\|\omega_{\xi}(\bm{\theta}_{k+1},\tau)\bm{g}(\tau\mid\bm{\theta}_{k+1})-\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k+1})\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]
≤𝔼τ∼ξ​p𝜽k+1+(1−ξ)​p𝜽k​[‖ωξ​(𝜽k+1,τ)​𝒈​(τ∣𝜽k+1)‖22]\displaystyle\qquad\leq\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\xi p_{\bm{\theta}_{k+1}}+(1-\xi)p_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}}\left[\left\|\omega_{\xi}(\bm{\theta}_{k+1},\tau)\bm{g}(\tau\mid\bm{\theta}_{k+1})\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]
=𝔼τ∼p𝜽k+1​[ωξ​(𝜽k+1,τ)​‖𝒈⁡(τ∣𝜽k+1)‖22]\displaystyle\qquad=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p_{\bm{\theta}_{k+1}}}\left[\omega_{\xi}(\bm{\theta}_{k+1},\tau)\|\bm{g}(\tau\mid\bm{\theta}_{k+1})\|_{2}^{2}\right]
≤1ξ​𝔼τ∼p𝜽k+1​[‖𝒈⁡(τ∣𝜽k+1)‖22]≤ν2ξ.\displaystyle\qquad\leq\frac{1}{\xi}\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p_{\bm{\theta}_{k+1}}}\left[\|\bm{g}(\tau\mid\bm{\theta}_{k+1})\|_{2}^{2}\right]\leq\frac{\nu^{2}}{\xi}.

The equality follows by canceling one importance weight against the mixture distribution. The final inequalities use ωξ​(𝜽k+1,τ)≤1/ξ\omega_{\xi}(\bm{\theta}_{k+1},\tau)\leq 1/\xi and the uncentered second-moment bound established in the proof of Lemma D.1. Substituting these bounds into the conditional estimation error inequality gives:

𝔼[∥∇^𝜽†J(𝜽k+1)−∇𝜽J(𝜽k+1)∥22∣ℱk,ck=0]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\|\widehat{\nabla}^{\dagger}_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k+1})-\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k+1})\|_{2}^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{k},c_{k}=0\right]
≤(1−α)2​‖∇^𝜽†​J​(𝜽k)−∇𝜽J​(𝜽k)‖22+2​(1−α)2​C†,ωB​‖𝜽k+1−𝜽k‖22+2​α2​ν2ξ​B.\displaystyle\qquad\leq(1-\alpha)^{2}\|\widehat{\nabla}^{\dagger}_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k})-\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k})\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{2(1-\alpha)^{2}C_{\dagger,\omega}}{B}\|\bm{\theta}_{k+1}-\bm{\theta}_{k}\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{2\alpha^{2}\nu^{2}}{\xi B}.

Taking expectation over the preceding history, and using the independence of ckc_{k} from that history, yields,

𝔼⁡[‖∇^𝜽†​J​(𝜽k+1)−∇𝜽J​(𝜽k+1)‖22∣ck=0]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\|\widehat{\nabla}^{\dagger}_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k+1})-\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k+1})\|_{2}^{2}\mid c_{k}=0\right]
≤(1−α)2​Δk+2​(1−α)2​C†,ωB​𝔼​[‖𝜽k+1−𝜽k‖22]+2​α2​ν2ξ​B.\displaystyle\qquad\leq(1-\alpha)^{2}\Delta_{k}+\frac{2(1-\alpha)^{2}C_{\dagger,\omega}}{B}\mathbb{E}\left[\|\bm{\theta}_{k+1}-\bm{\theta}_{k}\|_{2}^{2}\right]+\frac{2\alpha^{2}\nu^{2}}{\xi B}.

Summing the two branches, we obtain,

Δk+1\displaystyle\Delta_{k+1} ≤p⁡(ν2N)+(1−p)​[(1−α)2​Δk+2​(1−α)2​C†,ωB​𝔼​[‖𝜽k+1−𝜽k‖22]+2​α2​ν2ξ​B]\displaystyle\leq p\left(\frac{\nu^{2}}{N}\right)+(1-p)\left[(1-\alpha)^{2}\Delta_{k}+\frac{2(1-\alpha)^{2}C_{\dagger,\omega}}{B}\mathbb{E}\left[\|\bm{\theta}_{k+1}-\bm{\theta}_{k}\|_{2}^{2}\right]+\frac{2\alpha^{2}\nu^{2}}{\xi B}\right]
=(1−p)​(1−α)2​Δk+2​(1−p)​(1−α)2​C†,ωB​𝔼​[‖𝜽k+1−𝜽k‖22]+p​ν2N+2​α2​(1−p)​ν2ξ​B.\displaystyle=(1-p)(1-\alpha)^{2}\Delta_{k}+\frac{2(1-p)(1-\alpha)^{2}C_{\dagger,\omega}}{B}\mathbb{E}\left[\|\bm{\theta}_{k+1}-\bm{\theta}_{k}\|_{2}^{2}\right]+\frac{p\nu^{2}}{N}+\frac{2\alpha^{2}(1-p)\nu^{2}}{\xi B}.

Δk+1≤(1−λ)​Δk+2​(1−λ)​C†,ωB​𝔼​[‖𝜽k+1−𝜽k‖22]+(pN+4​α2​(1−p)B)​ν2.\displaystyle\Delta_{k+1}\leq(1-\lambda)\Delta_{k}+\frac{2(1-\lambda)C_{\dagger,\omega}}{B}\mathbb{E}\left[\|\bm{\theta}_{k+1}-\bm{\theta}_{k}\|_{2}^{2}\right]+\left(\frac{p}{N}+\frac{4\alpha^{2}(1-p)}{B}\right)\nu^{2}.

∎

Appendix E Convergence

In this section, the last-iterate global-convergence guarantee for the LVR-PG algorithm is provided. In particular, Theorem 5.1 provides the sample-complexity for the LVR-PG framework, and while Corollaries E.1 and E.2 provide the sample complexities DEF-PAGE-PG and DEF-STORM-PG as instantiations of LVR-PG. Finally, Corollary 5.1 provides the convergence result for LVR-PG when instantiated for Fisher-non-degenerate policies. The lemmas used to prove the results of this section are provided in Appendix D and H.

E.1 Proof of Theorem 5.1

Here, the proof of Theorem 5.1 is provided. Leveraging the proof technique in Theorem 4.5 of Xu et al. (2019) for projected gradient ascent, we construct a recurrence that depends on both the sub-optimality gap and the variance of the estimator. We show that this recurrence achieves minimax-optimal sample complexity up to logarithmic factors and horizon terms.

See 5.1

Proof.

Following the proof of Theorem 4.5 by Xu et al. (2019), we start by redefining the objective function to incorporate the constraint set via the non-smooth indicator function 𝕀Θ​(𝜽)\mathbb{I}_{\Theta}(\bm{\theta}), introducing 𝒥⁡(𝜽)≔J⁡(𝜽)−𝕀Θ​(𝜽)\mathcal{J}(\bm{\theta})\coloneqq J(\bm{\theta})-\mathbb{I}_{\Theta}(\bm{\theta}). We formally define the generalized gradient mapping as 𝒢η(𝜽)≔1η(𝒫Θ(𝜽+η∇J(𝜽))−𝜽)\mathcal{G}_{\eta}(\bm{\theta})\coloneqq\frac{1}{\eta}(\mathcal{P}_{\Theta}(\bm{\theta}+\eta\nabla J(\bm{\theta}))-\bm{\theta}). we have arg​max𝜽∈ℝdΘ⁡𝒥⁡(𝜽)=arg​max𝜽∈Θ⁡J⁡(𝜽)≔𝜽∗\text{arg}\max_{\bm{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\Theta}}}\mathcal{J}(\bm{\theta})=\text{arg}\max_{\bm{\theta}\in\Theta}J(\bm{\theta})\coloneqq\bm{\theta}^{*}. Considering an iteration k∈⟦K⟧k\in\llbracket K\rrbracket, the parameter update applies projected stochastic gradient ascent: 𝜽k+1=𝒫Θ​(𝜽k+η​∇^𝜽†​J​(𝜽k))\bm{\theta}_{k+1}=\mathcal{P}_{\Theta}(\bm{\theta}_{k}+\eta\widehat{\nabla}^{\dagger}_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k})). From the LL-smoothness of J⁡(𝜽)J(\bm{\theta}) obtained in Lemma D.2, we can write the ascent lemma as follows:

Reversing the sign, applying the total expectation, and substituting the suboptimality rk≔𝔼⁡[𝒥~∗−𝒥⁡(𝜽k)]r_{k}\coloneqq\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\mathcal{J}}^{*}-\mathcal{J}(\bm{\theta}_{k})] and the estimation error Δk≔𝔼⁡[‖∇^𝜽†​J​(𝜽k)−∇𝜽J​(𝜽k)‖22]\Delta_{k}\coloneqq\mathbb{E}[\|\widehat{\nabla}^{\dagger}_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k})-\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k})\|_{2}^{2}], we obtain the projected suboptimality recurrence:

From Lemma D.4, the unified variance recurrence uses the effective decay rate λ≔1−(1−p)​(1−α)2\lambda\coloneqq 1-(1-p)(1-\alpha)^{2} and noise floor Cν≔(pN+4​α2​(1−p)B)​ν2C_{\nu}\coloneqq\left(\frac{p}{N}+\frac{4\alpha^{2}(1-p)}{B}\right)\nu^{2}. The variance recurrence is:

K≥max⁡{32μ​η​ϵ,4λ}​log+​2​Φ0ϵ.\displaystyle K\geq\max\left\{\frac{32}{\mu\eta\epsilon},\frac{4}{\lambda}\right\}\log_{+}\frac{2\Phi_{0}}{\epsilon}. (15)

To guarantee convergence to the target accuracy ϵ\epsilon, the noise term must satisfy two conditions. The first condition e≤a​ϵ22e\leq a\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{2} requires 3​η​Cν2​λ≤μ​η​ϵ264\frac{3\eta C_{\nu}}{2\lambda}\leq\frac{\mu\eta\epsilon^{2}}{64}, which simplifies to bounding the noise floor Cν≤μ​λ​ϵ296C_{\nu}\leq\frac{\mu\lambda\epsilon^{2}}{96}. The second condition e≤b​ϵ2e\leq b\frac{\epsilon}{2} requires 3​η​Cν2​λ≤λ​ϵ8\frac{3\eta C_{\nu}}{2\lambda}\leq\frac{\lambda\epsilon}{8}, which dictates the maximum stable learning rate η≤λ2​ϵ12​Cν\eta\leq\frac{\lambda^{2}\epsilon}{12C_{\nu}}. We satisfy the first accuracy condition Cν≤μ​λ​ϵ296C_{\nu}\leq\frac{\mu\lambda\epsilon^{2}}{96} by configuring the algorithmic parameters such that each of the two additive terms in Cν=(pN+4​α2​(1−p)B)​ν2C_{\nu}=\left(\frac{p}{N}+\frac{4\alpha^{2}(1-p)}{B}\right)\nu^{2} is independently bounded by half of the target limit, μ​λ​ϵ2192\frac{\mu\lambda\epsilon^{2}}{192}. With the unified decay rate λ=p+(1−p)​(2​α−α2)\lambda=p+(1-p)(2\alpha-\alpha^{2}), we evaluate both terms to define the feasible geometric region.

First Term of CνC_{\nu} and Batch Size.

Observing that 2​α−α2≥02\alpha-\alpha^{2}\geq 0, we establish the lower bound λ≥p\lambda\geq p. It is therefore sufficient to enforce:

p​ν2N≤μ​p​ϵ2192⟹N≥192​ν2μ​ϵ2.\displaystyle\frac{p\nu^{2}}{N}\leq\frac{\mu p\epsilon^{2}}{192}\implies N\geq\frac{192\nu^{2}}{\mu\epsilon^{2}}.

To minimize sample cost while satisfying this requirement, we select a full batch size N=Θ⁡(ϵ−2)N=\Theta(\epsilon^{-2}) and initialize with N0=N=Θ⁡(ϵ−2)N_{0}=N=\Theta(\epsilon^{-2}).

Second Term of CνC_{\nu} and Momentum.

Observing that 2​α−α2=α⁡(2−α)≥α2\alpha-\alpha^{2}=\alpha(2-\alpha)\geq\alpha for any α∈(0,1]\alpha\in(0,1], and dropping the positive pp term from λ\lambda, we obtain the lower bound λ≥(1−p)​α\lambda\geq(1-p)\alpha. Substituting this lower bound into the right-hand side, it is strictly sufficient to require:

4​α2​(1−p)​ν2B≤μ⁡(1−p)​α​ϵ2192.\displaystyle\frac{4\alpha^{2}(1-p)\nu^{2}}{B}\leq\frac{\mu(1-p)\alpha\epsilon^{2}}{192}.

Because α>0\alpha>0, we divide both sides by the common factor α⁡(1−p)\alpha(1-p) to directly isolate α\alpha:

4​α​ν2B≤μ​ϵ2192⟹α≤μ​B​ϵ2768​ν2.\displaystyle\frac{4\alpha\nu^{2}}{B}\leq\frac{\mu\epsilon^{2}}{192}\implies\alpha\leq\frac{\mu B\epsilon^{2}}{768\nu^{2}}.

This establishes the strict upper bound α=𝒪⁡(B​ϵ2)\alpha=\mathcal{O}(B\epsilon^{2}).

Expected Sample Cost and Refresh Probability.

We choose p,α≥0p,\alpha\geq 0 such that

p+α=μ​B​ϵ2768​ν2.\displaystyle p+\alpha=\frac{\mu B\epsilon^{2}}{768\nu^{2}}.

This ensures the momentum constraint established above. For sufficiently small ϵ\epsilon, we have p+α≤1/2p+\alpha\leq 1/2, and hence

p+α≤λ=p+(1−p)​(2​α−α2)≤p+2​α≤2​(p+α).\displaystyle p+\alpha\leq\lambda=p+(1-p)(2\alpha-\alpha^{2})\leq p+2\alpha\leq 2(p+\alpha).

Therefore, λ=Θ⁡(μ​B​ϵ2/ν2)\lambda=\Theta(\mu B\epsilon^{2}/\nu^{2}), with universal implicit constants. Moreover, since p≤μ​B​ϵ2/(768​ν2)p\leq\mu B\epsilon^{2}/(768\nu^{2}),

p​N+(1−p)​B\displaystyle pN+(1-p)B ≤μ​B​ϵ2768​ν2​(192​ν2μ​ϵ2+1)+B\displaystyle\leq\frac{\mu B\epsilon^{2}}{768\nu^{2}}\left(\frac{192\nu^{2}}{\mu\epsilon^{2}}+1\right)+B
≤5​B4+12=𝒪⁡(B).\displaystyle\leq\frac{5B}{4}+\frac{1}{2}=\mathcal{O}(B).

Learning Rate.

To achieve the optimal total sample complexity n=𝒪~​(ϵ−2)n=\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-2}), and match the lower-bound established by Theorem 3.1 up to logarithmic factors, the iteration complexity KK must be bounded by 𝒪⁡((B​ϵ2)−1)\mathcal{O}((B\epsilon^{2})^{-1}). This bound limits the total number of optimization steps to guarantee that the cumulative sample cost of the 𝒪⁡(B)\mathcal{O}(B) per-iteration updates does not breach the optimal 𝒪~​(ϵ−2)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-2}) global sample complexity. Given the initial batch N0=Θ⁡(ϵ−2)N_{0}=\Theta(\epsilon^{-2}) and an expected per-iteration sample cost bounded by 𝒪⁡(B)\mathcal{O}(B), the number of iterations must satisfy K⋅𝒪⁡(B)≤𝒪~​(ϵ−2)K\cdot\mathcal{O}(B)\leq\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-2}), which mandates K≤𝒪⁡((B​ϵ2)−1)K\leq\mathcal{O}((B\epsilon^{2})^{-1}). The sufficient iteration budget in Equation (15) contains the estimator-decay term 4/λ4/\lambda. To keep this term within the desired iteration budget 𝒪⁡((B​ϵ2)−1)\mathcal{O}((B\epsilon^{2})^{-1}), we impose λ=Ω⁡(B​ϵ2)\lambda=\Omega(B\epsilon^{2}). This condition controls the iteration complexity of our analysis; it does not establish that configurations with smaller λ\lambda necessarily require more iterations to reach the target accuracy. Expanding the definition of the decay rate yields: λ=1−(1−p)​(1−α)2=p+2​α−α2−2​p​α+p​α2\lambda=1-(1-p)(1-\alpha)^{2}=p+2\alpha-\alpha^{2}-2p\alpha+p\alpha^{2}. Since the upper bounds p=𝒪⁡(B​ϵ2)p=\mathcal{O}(B\epsilon^{2}) and α=𝒪⁡(B​ϵ2)\alpha=\mathcal{O}(B\epsilon^{2}) are established, the higher-order terms α2\alpha^{2}, p​αp\alpha, and p​α2p\alpha^{2} scale as 𝒪⁡(B2​ϵ4)\mathcal{O}(B^{2}\epsilon^{4}) or smaller. Consequently, for sufficiently small target accuracy ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0, the decay rate is dominated by its linear components, reducing asymptotically to λ=p+2​α−𝒪⁡(B2​ϵ4)\lambda=p+2\alpha-\mathcal{O}(B^{2}\epsilon^{4}). To satisfy the λ=Ω⁡(B​ϵ2)\lambda=\Omega(B\epsilon^{2}) decay floor, these dominant terms must jointly fulfill the geometric condition p+α=Ω⁡(B​ϵ2)p+\alpha=\Omega(B\epsilon^{2}). For any configuration (p,α)(p,\alpha) satisfying this combined system of bounds, the decay rate and noise floor scale precisely as λ=Θ⁡(B​ϵ2)\lambda=\Theta(B\epsilon^{2}) and Cν=Θ⁡(B​ϵ4)C_{\nu}=\Theta(B\epsilon^{4}), respectively. We evaluate the remaining step-size restrictions using these asymptotic rates. The last-iterate stability condition η≤λ2​ϵ12​Cν\eta\leq\frac{\lambda^{2}\epsilon}{12C_{\nu}} resolves to η≤Θ⁡(B​ϵ)\eta\leq\Theta(B\epsilon). Concurrently, the variance recurrence threshold evaluates to λ​B12​(1−λ)​C†,ω=Θ⁡(B​ϵ)\sqrt{\frac{\lambda B}{12(1-\lambda)C_{\dagger,\omega}}}=\Theta(B\epsilon). By explicitly selecting the step size η\eta to match this scaling alongside the LL-smoothness limit, all stability requirements are unconditionally satisfied:

η=min⁡{14​L,λ2​ϵ12​Cν,λ​B24​(1−λ)​C†,ω}=Θ⁡(B​ϵ).\displaystyle\eta=\min\left\{\frac{1}{4L},\frac{\lambda^{2}\epsilon}{12C_{\nu}},\sqrt{\frac{\lambda B}{24(1-\lambda)C_{\dagger,\omega}}}\right\}=\Theta(B\epsilon).

Sample Complexity.

With these conditions established, Lemma H.2 guarantees that it suffices to choose the number of iterations as:

K=⌈max⁡{32μ​η​ϵ,4λ}​log+​2​Φ0ϵ⌉.\displaystyle K=\left\lceil\max\left\{\frac{32}{\mu\eta\epsilon},\frac{4}{\lambda}\right\}\log_{+}\frac{2\Phi_{0}}{\epsilon}\right\rceil.

Substituting our choice of η\eta into the iteration bound gives:

K=⌈max⁡{128​Lμ​ϵ,384​Cνμ​λ2​ϵ2,32​24​(1−λ)​C†,ωμ​ϵ​λ​B,4λ}​log+​2​Φ0ϵ⌉.\displaystyle K=\left\lceil\max\left\{\frac{128L}{\mu\epsilon},\frac{384C_{\nu}}{\mu\lambda^{2}\epsilon^{2}},\frac{32\sqrt{24(1-\lambda)C_{\dagger,\omega}}}{\mu\epsilon\sqrt{\lambda B}},\frac{4}{\lambda}\right\}\log_{+}\frac{2\Phi_{0}}{\epsilon}\right\rceil.

The noise constraint Cν≤μ​λ​ϵ2/96C_{\nu}\leq\mu\lambda\epsilon^{2}/96 implies

384​Cνμ​λ2​ϵ2≤384μ​λ2​ϵ2​μ​λ​ϵ296=4λ.\displaystyle\frac{384C_{\nu}}{\mu\lambda^{2}\epsilon^{2}}\leq\frac{384}{\mu\lambda^{2}\epsilon^{2}}\frac{\mu\lambda\epsilon^{2}}{96}=\frac{4}{\lambda}.

Thus, this term is absorbed by the estimator-decay term. Moreover, the established bound λ≥μ​B​ϵ2/(768​ν2)\lambda\geq\mu B\epsilon^{2}/(768\nu^{2}) yields

4λ≤3072​ν2μ​B​ϵ2.\displaystyle\frac{4}{\lambda}\leq\frac{3072\nu^{2}}{\mu B\epsilon^{2}}.

Using the same lower bound on λ\lambda and 1−λ≤11-\lambda\leq 1, the variance-stability term satisfies

32​24​(1−λ)​C†,ωμ​ϵ​λ​B\displaystyle\frac{32\sqrt{24(1-\lambda)C_{\dagger,\omega}}}{\mu\epsilon\sqrt{\lambda B}} ≤32​24​C†,ωμ​ϵ​768​ν2μ​B2​ϵ2\displaystyle\leq\frac{32\sqrt{24C_{\dagger,\omega}}}{\mu\epsilon}\sqrt{\frac{768\nu^{2}}{\mu B^{2}\epsilon^{2}}}
=3072​2​ν​C†,ωμ3/2​B​ϵ2.\displaystyle=\frac{3072\sqrt{2}\,\nu\sqrt{C_{\dagger,\omega}}}{\mu^{3/2}B\epsilon^{2}}.

Combining these bounds, absorbing numerical constants and logarithmic factors, and accounting for the ceiling, we obtain:

K=𝒪~​(1+Lμ​ϵ+ν2μ​B​ϵ2+ν​C†,ωμ3/2​B​ϵ2).\displaystyle K=\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(1+\frac{L}{\mu\epsilon}+\frac{\nu^{2}}{\mu B\epsilon^{2}}+\frac{\nu\sqrt{C_{\dagger,\omega}}}{\mu^{3/2}B\epsilon^{2}}\right).

The expected total sample complexity nn is determined by the initial batch size N0N_{0} plus the sum of the expected batch sizes drawn over the KK iterations:

n=N0+K⁡(p​N+(1−p)​B).\displaystyle n=N_{0}+K(pN+(1-p)B).

By substituting N0=⌈192​ν2/(μ​ϵ2)⌉N_{0}=\left\lceil 192\nu^{2}/(\mu\epsilon^{2})\right\rceil, the iteration bound above, and the bounded per-iteration cost p​N+(1−p)​B=𝒪⁡(B)pN+(1-p)B=\mathcal{O}(B), we obtain:

n=𝒪~​(1+B+B​Lμ​ϵ+ν2μ​ϵ2+ν​C†,ωμ3/2​ϵ2).\displaystyle n=\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(1+B+\frac{BL}{\mu\epsilon}+\frac{\nu^{2}}{\mu\epsilon^{2}}+\frac{\nu\sqrt{C_{\dagger,\omega}}}{\mu^{3/2}\epsilon^{2}}\right).

Thus, for fixed BB and fixed positive problem-dependent constants, the complexity is n=𝒪~​(ϵ−2)n=\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-2}) as ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0. To establish the asymptotic dependence on the reward bounds and the effective horizon, we substitute the problem-dependent constants. From Lemma D.1, the GPOMDP second-moment bound scales as ν2=𝒪⁡(Rmax2​(1−γ)−3)\nu^{2}=\mathcal{O}(R_{\max}^{2}(1-\gamma)^{-3}). From Lemma B.1, the defensive mean-squared smoothness constant scales as C†,ω=𝒪⁡(Rmax2​(1−γ)−5)C_{\dagger,\omega}=\mathcal{O}(R_{\max}^{2}(1-\gamma)^{-5}). Substituting these bounds into the terms proportional to ϵ−2\epsilon^{-2}, and using μ=χ−2\mu=\chi^{-2}, yields:

n=𝒪~​(Rmax2ϵ2​[χ2(1−γ)3+χ3(1−γ)4]),\displaystyle n=\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\frac{R_{\max}^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}\left[\frac{\chi^{2}}{(1-\gamma)^{3}}+\frac{\chi^{3}}{(1-\gamma)^{4}}\right]\right),

where the policy-regularity and defensive-mixture constants are treated as fixed. This establishes the minimax-optimal dependence on ϵ\epsilon, up to logarithmic factors, while retaining the explicit dependence on the WGD constant and the effective horizon. ∎

E.2 Corollaries of Theorem 5.1

Here, we consider the sample complexity of two specific instantiations of LVR-PG: DEF-PAGE-PG and DEF-STORM-PG. First, we show how the parameter λ\lambda, defined in Lemma B.1, changes setting the α\alpha and pp parameters. Then, we study the batch size NN, mini-batch size BB and learning rate η\eta to recover the desired sample complexity.

Corollary E.1 (Sample Complexity of DEF-PAGE-PG).

Under Assumptions 3.1–3.2, for a fixed mini-batch size B≥1B\geq 1 and sufficiently small target accuracy ϵ>0\epsilon>0, through an appropriate choice of the algorithmic parameters (full batch size NN, initial batch size N0N_{0}, refresh probability pp, and learning rate η\eta), DEF-PAGE-PG with α=0\alpha=0 guarantees J∗−𝔼⁡[J⁡(𝛉k)]≤ψ+ϵJ^{*}-\mathbb{E}[J(\bm{\theta}_{k})]\leq\psi+\epsilon with a sample complexity of at most:

n\displaystyle n =N0+K⁡(1+B−BN)\displaystyle=N_{0}+K\left(1+B-\frac{B}{N}\right)
=𝒪~​(Rmax2ϵ2​[χ2(1−γ)3+χ3(1−γ)4]).\displaystyle=\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\frac{R_{\max}^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}\left[\frac{\chi^{2}}{(1-\gamma)^{3}}+\frac{\chi^{3}}{(1-\gamma)^{4}}\right]\right).

η≤μ​B4608​ν2​CDEF,ω​ϵ≤B24​N​CDEF,ω.\displaystyle\eta\leq\sqrt{\frac{\mu B}{4608\nu^{2}C_{\texttt{DEF},\omega}}}\epsilon\leq\sqrt{\frac{B}{24NC_{\texttt{DEF},\omega}}}.

λ2​ϵ12​Cν=p​N​ϵ12​ν2=ϵ12​ν2.\displaystyle\frac{\lambda^{2}\epsilon}{12C_{\nu}}=\frac{pN\epsilon}{12\nu^{2}}=\frac{\epsilon}{12\nu^{2}}.

Defining

cη≔min⁡{112​ν2,μ​B4608​ν2​CDEF,ω},\displaystyle c_{\eta}\coloneqq\min\left\{\frac{1}{12\nu^{2}},\sqrt{\frac{\mu B}{4608\nu^{2}C_{\texttt{DEF},\omega}}}\right\},

we therefore select η=min⁡{1/(4​L),cη​ϵ}\eta=\min\{1/(4L),c_{\eta}\epsilon\}. n=𝒪~​(Rmax2ϵ2​[χ2(1−γ)3+χ3(1−γ)4]),\displaystyle n=\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\frac{R_{\max}^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}\left[\frac{\chi^{2}}{(1-\gamma)^{3}}+\frac{\chi^{3}}{(1-\gamma)^{4}}\right]\right),

Appendix F Sample Complexity under Fisher-non-Degeneracy

While Theorem 5.1 establishes the sample complexity bounds under the abstract weak gradient domination condition, we apply Assumptions C.2 and C.1 to apply Lemma C.1. Note that, in the FND setting, we consider the unconstrained parameter space Θ=ℝd\Theta=\mathbb{R}^{d}.

See 5.1

Proof.

The result follows directly from Theorem 5.1 by applying the Fisher-induced Gradient Domination Lemma. Specifically, the lemma establishes that under Assumptions C.2 and C.1, the Weak Gradient Domination condition holds with the constants χ=C1/μF\chi=C_{1}/\mu_{F} and ψ=ϵbias​κ/(1−γ)\psi=\sqrt{\epsilon_{\text{bias}}}\kappa/(1-\gamma). Substituting these specific values into the optimality gap and the general sample complexity bound of Theorem 5.1 immediately yields the stated result. ∎

Appendix G Lower-Bound

See 3.1

Before starting with the proof of Theorem 3.1, we describe it and its difference from previous works. The proof relies on the information-theoretic framework for minimax lower bounds and uses Le Cam’s two-point method. While the hard instance construction shares topological similarities with the absorbing MDPs introduced by Azar et al. (2013), we accommodate the specific geometry of policy optimization. While Azar et al. (2013) establishes lower bounds for unconstrained tabular reinforcement learning, in our proof, we consider a constrained continuous policy parametrization, θ∈[α,1−α]\theta\in[\alpha,1-\alpha]. This domain restriction is the critical mechanism that enforces Assumption 3.1. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this constrained geometry satisfies Assumption 3.2 with χ=4/3\chi=4/3 and ψ=0\psi=0, avoiding vanishing gradients at the optimal boundaries.

To establish a fundamental lower bound on the sample complexity of any learning algorithm, we must construct an adversarial scenario in which making the correct decision is statistically difficult, yet an incorrect guess incurs a penalty. We achieve this by designing two nearly identical MDPs, ℳ1\mathcal{M}_{1} and ℳ2\mathcal{M}_{2}. These instances differ strictly by a small perturbation δ\delta in the transition probabilities, making them difficult to distinguish, yet they require mutually exclusive optimal policies. We first quantify the sub-optimality gap to show that if an algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} fails to identify the true underlying MDP and selects a parameter favouring the wrong action, it suffers a performance penalty of at least Ω⁡(δ​(1−γ)−1)\Omega(\delta(1-\gamma)^{-1}). By tuning this ”wrong-action” penalty to perfectly match our target accuracy threshold ϵ\epsilon, we isolate the required perturbation scale to δ=𝒪⁡(ϵ​(1−γ)2)\delta=\mathcal{O}(\epsilon(1-\gamma)^{2}).

Because a valid 𝒜\mathcal{A} must guarantee ϵ\epsilon-optimality across all instances, it is forced to determine whether it is interacting with ℳ1\mathcal{M}_{1} or ℳ2\mathcal{M}_{2}. If it collects too few samples, the trajectory distributions of the two MDPs remain virtually identical, and the algorithm will inevitably guess wrong with high probability, thereby suffering the tuned ϵ\epsilon penalty. We formalize this through Le Cam’s method, which implies that, to reliably distinguish the two instances, the total Kullback-Leibler divergence between their nn-trajectory distributions must exceed a given threshold.

Finally, we establish how much data is required to cross this threshold by analytically upper-bounding the KL divergence. We show that the divergence accumulates to at most 𝒪⁡(n​δ2​(1−γ)−2)\mathcal{O}(n\delta^{2}(1-\gamma)^{-2}). Substituting our chosen δ\delta into this upper bound and solving for the sample size nn reveals that the minimum amount of data required to distinguish the instances, and thus avoid the sub-optimality penalty, is exactly Ω⁡((1−γ)−2​Rmax2​ϵ−2)\Omega((1-\gamma)^{-2}R_{\max}^{2}\epsilon^{-2}).

Proof.

The proof is subdivided into several parts.

Part I: Construction of the Hard Instance.

We consider a class of MDPs consisting of two instances, ℳ∈{ℳ1,ℳ2}\mathcal{M}\in\{\mathcal{M}_{1},\mathcal{M}_{2}\}, with state space 𝒮={s,s¯}\mathcal{S}=\{s,\bar{s}\} and action space 𝒜={a0,a1}\mathcal{A}=\{a_{0},a_{1}\}. The state s¯\bar{s} is an absorbing state where any action a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A} yields a deterministic self-transition with zero reward, meaning P⁡(s¯|s¯,a)=1P(\bar{s}|\bar{s},a)=1 and R⁡(s¯,a,s¯)=0R(\bar{s},a,\bar{s})=0. In the initial state ss, taking an action aa triggers a self-transition to ss with probability pap_{a}, yielding a reward of RmaxR_{\max}, and transitions to the absorbing state s¯\bar{s} with probability 1−pa1-p_{a}, yielding RmaxR_{\max}. The two instances differ strictly in the transition probabilities from the initial state ss. For the instance ℳ1\mathcal{M}_{1}, we set pa0=p+δp_{a_{0}}=p+\delta and pa1=pp_{a_{1}}=p, making a0a_{0} the optimal action. Conversely, for the instance ℳ2\mathcal{M}_{2}, we set pa0=pp_{a_{0}}=p and pa1=p+δp_{a_{1}}=p+\delta, making a1a_{1} the optimal action. To ensure the transition probabilities remain valid while capturing the lower-bound complexity dependence on the effective horizon, we define the base transition probability as p=1−1−γγp=1-\frac{1-\gamma}{\gamma}. Consequently, to satisfy the requirement that p+δ≤1p+\delta\leq 1, the perturbation parameter δ\delta is strictly bounded by δ≤1−γ2​γ\delta\leq\frac{1-\gamma}{2\gamma}.

We consider a direct policy parametrization in which the scalar parameter θ\theta determines the probability of selecting the action a0a_{0} in the initial state ss. For the binary action space 𝒜={a0,a1}\mathcal{A}=\{a_{0},a_{1}\}, the policy is defined as:

πθ​(a∣s)\displaystyle\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s) ={θif ​a=a0,1−θotherwise.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\theta&\text{if }a=a_{0},\\ 1-\theta&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

Here, we check that the policy class we have choosen satisfies Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2. To ensure the policy space satisfies the regularity constraints of Assumption 3.1, we restrict the parameter domain to Θ=[α,1−α]\Theta=[\alpha,1-\alpha] for a strictly positive constant α∈(0,1/2)\alpha\in(0,1/2). The score function is given by:

∇θ​log​πθ​(a∣s)\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s) ={1θif ​a=a0,−11−θotherwhise.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{\theta}&\text{if }a=a_{0},\\ -\frac{1}{1-\theta}&\text{otherwhise}.\end{cases}

supa∈𝒜‖∇θ​log​πθ​(a∣s)‖2\displaystyle\sup_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\big\|\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)\big\|_{2} =maxθ∈[α,1−α]⁡max⁡{1θ,11−θ}=1α.\displaystyle=\max_{\theta\in[\alpha,1-\alpha]}\max\left\{\frac{1}{\theta},\frac{1}{1-\theta}\right\}=\frac{1}{\alpha}.

Part III: Value Gap and Choice of Perturbation.

To establish the statistical hardness, we must ensure that failing to identify the correct MDP results in a substantial performance penalty. Specifically, we require that if an algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} outputs a policy that favors the wrong action, the sub-optimality gap is at least 4​ϵ4\epsilon.

In instance ℳ1\mathcal{M}_{1}, the optimal parameter is θ∗=1−α>1/2\theta^{*}=1-\alpha>1/2. The algorithm outputs a highly sub-optimal policy if it incorrectly favors action a1a_{1}, which occurs when θ≤1/2\theta\leq 1/2. We evaluate the sub-optimality gap for ℳ1\mathcal{M}_{1} given θ≤1/2\theta\leq 1/2 to find a strict lower bound. From the previous derivation, the gap is:

J∗,(1)−J(1)​(θ)\displaystyle J^{*,(1)}-J^{(1)}(\theta) =γ​Rmax​(1−α−θ)​δ(1−γ⁡(p+(1−α)​δ))​(1−γ⁡(p+θ​δ)).\displaystyle=\frac{\gamma R_{\max}(1-\alpha-\theta)\delta}{(1-\gamma(p+(1-\alpha)\delta))(1-\gamma(p+\theta\delta))}.

To lower-bound this gap, we lower-bound the numerator and upper-bound the denominator. Because θ≤1/2\theta\leq 1/2, the term (1−α−θ)(1-\alpha-\theta) is bounded below by (1/2−α)(1/2-\alpha). Furthermore, since we established the condition γ≥1/2\gamma\geq 1/2 to ensure valid transition probabilities, we substitute γ=1/2\gamma=1/2 to strictly lower-bound the numerator and remove its dependence on γ\gamma:

γ​Rmax​(1−α−θ)​δ\displaystyle\gamma R_{\max}(1-\alpha-\theta)\delta ≥12​Rmax​(12−α)​δ=Rmax​(1−2​α)​δ4.\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{2}R_{\max}\left(\frac{1}{2}-\alpha\right)\delta=\frac{R_{\max}(1-2\alpha)\delta}{4}.

For the denominator, since θ​δ≥0\theta\delta\geq 0 and (1−α)​δ≥0(1-\alpha)\delta\geq 0, the effective horizon terms are strictly upper-bounded by the baseline effective horizon 1−γ​p=2​(1−γ)1-\gamma p=2(1-\gamma):

(1−γ⁡(p+(1−α)​δ))​(1−γ⁡(p+θ​δ))\displaystyle(1-\gamma(p+(1-\alpha)\delta))(1-\gamma(p+\theta\delta)) ≤(2​(1−γ))​(2​(1−γ))=4​(1−γ)2.\displaystyle\leq(2(1-\gamma))(2(1-\gamma))=4(1-\gamma)^{2}.

Combining these bounds, the sub-optimality gap for any parameter θ≤1/2\theta\leq 1/2 is bounded from below:

J∗,(1)−J(1)​(θ)\displaystyle J^{*,(1)}-J^{(1)}(\theta) ≥Rmax​(1−2​α)​δ44​(1−γ)2=Rmax​(1−2​α)​δ16​(1−γ)2.\displaystyle\geq\frac{\frac{R_{\max}(1-2\alpha)\delta}{4}}{4(1-\gamma)^{2}}=\frac{R_{\max}(1-2\alpha)\delta}{16(1-\gamma)^{2}}.

To enforce that this misidentification penalty is at least 4​ϵ4\epsilon, we equate this lower bound to 4​ϵ4\epsilon and solve for the perturbation parameter δ\delta:

Rmax​(1−2​α)​δ16​(1−γ)2\displaystyle\frac{R_{\max}(1-2\alpha)\delta}{16(1-\gamma)^{2}} =4​ϵ⟹δ=64​ϵ​(1−γ)2Rmax​(1−2​α).\displaystyle=4\epsilon\implies\delta=\frac{64\epsilon(1-\gamma)^{2}}{R_{\max}(1-2\alpha)}.

This specific choice of δ\delta enforces the required value gap while controlling the statistical indistinguishability of the instances. To satisfy the transition probability constraint δ≤1−γ2​γ\delta\leq\frac{1-\gamma}{2\gamma}, the target accuracy ϵ\epsilon must be sufficiently small:

64​ϵ​(1−γ)2Rmax​(1−2​α)≤1−γ2​γ⟹ϵ≤Rmax​(1−2​α)128​γ​(1−γ).\displaystyle\frac{64\epsilon(1-\gamma)^{2}}{R_{\max}(1-2\alpha)}\leq\frac{1-\gamma}{2\gamma}\implies\epsilon\leq\frac{R_{\max}(1-2\alpha)}{128\gamma(1-\gamma)}.

Part IV: Statistical Test and Information-Theoretic Lower Bound. We formulate the learning process as a statistical testing problem. Suppose an algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} interacts with an unknown instance ℳi\mathcal{M}_{i}, i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\}, collects a possibly random number of trajectories N𝒜N_{\mathcal{A}}, and subsequently outputs a parameter estimate θ^∈Θ\widehat{\theta}\in\Theta. The algorithm is not informed whether the underlying environment is ℳ1\mathcal{M}_{1} or ℳ2\mathcal{M}_{2}, and its policies may depend on all previously observed trajectories. For 𝒜\mathcal{A} to be considered a successful ϵ\epsilon-optimal algorithm on these instances, its expected suboptimality gap must satisfy

𝔼𝒜,ℳi​[J∗,(i)−J(i)​(θ^)]≤ϵ,i∈{1,2},\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M}_{i}}\left[J^{*,(i)}-J^{(i)}(\widehat{\theta})\right]\leq\epsilon,\qquad i\in\{1,2\},

where J∗,(i)=maxθ∈Θ⁡J(i)​(θ)J^{*,(i)}=\max_{\theta\in\Theta}J^{(i)}(\theta). We define the worst-case expected trajectory budget as

n:=maxi∈{1,2}⁡𝔼𝒜,ℳi​[N𝒜].\displaystyle n:=\max_{i\in\{1,2\}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M}_{i}}[N_{\mathcal{A}}].

We may assume that n<∞n<\infty, since otherwise the claimed lower bound holds trivially. Using the suboptimality bound derived in Part III, any output θ^<1/2\widehat{\theta}<1/2 under ℳ1\mathcal{M}_{1} incurs a gap of at least 4​ϵ4\epsilon. Therefore,

ϵ\displaystyle\epsilon ≥𝔼𝒜,ℳ1​[J∗,(1)−J(1)​(θ^)]\displaystyle\geq\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M}_{1}}\left[J^{*,(1)}-J^{(1)}(\widehat{\theta})\right]
≥4​ϵ​ℙ𝒜,ℳ1​(θ^<12),\displaystyle\geq 4\epsilon\,\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M}_{1}}\left(\widehat{\theta}<\frac{1}{2}\right),

which implies:

ℙ𝒜,ℳ1​(θ^<12)≤14.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M}_{1}}\left(\widehat{\theta}<\frac{1}{2}\right)\leq\frac{1}{4}.

By symmetric reasoning under ℳ2\mathcal{M}_{2}, any output θ^≥1/2\widehat{\theta}\geq 1/2 incurs a gap of at least 4​ϵ4\epsilon, yielding,

ℙ𝒜,ℳ2​(θ^≥12)≤14.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M}_{2}}\left(\widehat{\theta}\geq\frac{1}{2}\right)\leq\frac{1}{4}.

Summing these error probabilities gives:

ℙ𝒜,ℳ1​(θ^<12)+ℙ𝒜,ℳ2​(θ^≥12)≤12.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M}_{1}}\left(\widehat{\theta}<\frac{1}{2}\right)+\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M}_{2}}\left(\widehat{\theta}\geq\frac{1}{2}\right)\leq\frac{1}{2}.

Let ℙ𝒜,ℳ1\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M}_{1}} and ℙ𝒜,ℳ2\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M}_{2}} denote the probability measures over the complete stopped interaction transcript under the two instances. This transcript includes the algorithm’s internal randomization, the observed trajectories, and its final output θ^\widehat{\theta}. Interpreting θ^≥1/2\widehat{\theta}\geq 1/2 as selecting ℳ1\mathcal{M}_{1}, Le Cam’s inequality gives:

ℙ𝒜,ℳ1​(θ^<12)+ℙ𝒜,ℳ2​(θ^≥12)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M}_{1}}\left(\widehat{\theta}<\frac{1}{2}\right)+\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M}_{2}}\left(\widehat{\theta}\geq\frac{1}{2}\right)
≥1−dTV​(ℙ𝒜,ℳ1,ℙ𝒜,ℳ2).\displaystyle\qquad\geq 1-d_{\mathrm{TV}}\!\left(\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M}_{1}},\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M}_{2}}\right).

Consequently, the total variation distance must be at least 1/21/2. Applying Pinsker’s inequality, we obtain,

12\displaystyle\frac{1}{2} ≤dTV​(ℙ𝒜,ℳ1,ℙ𝒜,ℳ2)\displaystyle\leq d_{\mathrm{TV}}\!\left(\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M}_{1}},\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M}_{2}}\right)
≤12​DKL​(ℙ𝒜,ℳ1∥ℙ𝒜,ℳ2),\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M}_{1}}\,\middle\|\,\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M}_{2}}\right)},

and hence:

DKL​(ℙ𝒜,ℳ1∥ℙ𝒜,ℳ2)≥12.\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M}_{1}}\,\middle\|\,\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M}_{2}}\right)\geq\frac{1}{2}.

To translate this information requirement into a trajectory complexity lower bound, we next upper-bound the divergence in terms of the expected number of collected trajectories.

Part V: Upper Bound on the KL Divergence. We upper-bound the KL divergence of the complete interaction transcript through the conditional chain rule for relative entropy. Conditional on the same realized history, the algorithm uses the same action-selection and stopping rules under both instances. Moreover, the initial state, reward function, and independent geometric termination mechanism are identical under ℳ1\mathcal{M}_{1} and ℳ2\mathcal{M}_{2}. Consequently, only the environment transition kernels contribute to the conditional KL divergence. We first bound the divergence contributed by a single transition. Since s¯\bar{s} is absorbing and possesses identical transition dynamics in both instances,

DKL(P(1)(⋅∣s¯,a)∥P(2)(⋅∣s¯,a))=0.\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(P^{(1)}(\cdot\mid\bar{s},a)\,\middle\|\,P^{(2)}(\cdot\mid\bar{s},a)\right)=0.

At the active state ss, the Bernoulli parameters under (ℳ1,ℳ2)(\mathcal{M}_{1},\mathcal{M}_{2}) are (p+δ,p)(p+\delta,p) for a0a_{0} and (p,p+δ)(p,p+\delta) for a1a_{1}. Using the standard inequality dKL(x∥y)≤(x−y)2/[y(1−y)]d_{\mathrm{KL}}(x\|y)\leq(x-y)^{2}/[y(1-y)], we obtain,

dKL(p+δ∥p)\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{KL}}(p+\delta\|p) ≤δ2p⁡(1−p),\displaystyle\leq\frac{\delta^{2}}{p(1-p)},
dKL(p∥p+δ)\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|p+\delta) ≤δ2(p+δ)​(1−p−δ).\displaystyle\leq\frac{\delta^{2}}{(p+\delta)(1-p-\delta)}.

Recall that p=(2​γ−1)/γp=(2\gamma-1)/\gamma, γ≥2/3\gamma\geq 2/3, and δ≤(1−γ)/(2​γ)\delta\leq(1-\gamma)/(2\gamma). These conditions imply:

p≥12,1−p=1−γγ,1−p−δ≥1−γ2​γ.\displaystyle p\geq\frac{1}{2},\qquad 1-p=\frac{1-\gamma}{\gamma},\qquad 1-p-\delta\geq\frac{1-\gamma}{2\gamma}.

Thus, both variance terms are bounded below by (1−γ)/(4​γ)(1-\gamma)/(4\gamma), yielding,

maxa∈{a0,a1}DKL(P(1)(⋅∣s,a)∥P(2)(⋅∣s,a))≤4​γ​δ21−γ≤4​δ21−γ.\displaystyle\max_{a\in\{a_{0},a_{1}\}}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(P^{(1)}(\cdot\mid s,a)\,\middle\|\,P^{(2)}(\cdot\mid s,a)\right)\leq\frac{4\gamma\delta^{2}}{1-\gamma}\leq\frac{4\delta^{2}}{1-\gamma}.

This bound holds uniformly over the selected action. Next, we bound the number of informative transitions within each trajectory. Let HjH_{j} denote the number of observed transitions in trajectory jj, and define:

Tj:=∑t=0Hj−1𝟏{sj,t=s},\displaystyle T_{j}:=\sum_{t=0}^{H_{j}-1}\mathbf{1}_{\{s_{j,t}=s\}},

where sj,ts_{j,t} and aj,ta_{j,t} denote the state and action at time tt of trajectory jj. Thus, TjT_{j} counts the observed transitions from the active state. Each trajectory starts at ss and follows the independent geometric termination protocol. We set Tj=0T_{j}=0 when trajectory jj is not collected. Let ℱj−1\mathcal{F}_{j-1} denote the history immediately before trajectory jj, including the algorithm’s decision whether to collect it. In particular, {N𝒜≥j}\{N_{\mathcal{A}}\geq j\} is ℱj−1\mathcal{F}_{j-1}-measurable. On this event, the conditional probability of remaining in ss after any active transition is at most p+δp+\delta, regardless of the selected action. The geometric termination mechanism can only reduce the number of observed active transitions. Consequently,

ℙ𝒜,ℳ1​(Tj>t∣ℱj−1)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M}_{1}}\left(T_{j}>t\mid\mathcal{F}_{j-1}\right) ≤(p+δ)t,t≥0,\displaystyle\leq(p+\delta)^{t},\qquad t\geq 0,
𝔼𝒜,ℳ1​[Tj∣ℱj−1]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M}_{1}}\left[T_{j}\mid\mathcal{F}_{j-1}\right] ≤∑t=0∞(p+δ)t\displaystyle\leq\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}(p+\delta)^{t}
=11−p−δ≤2​γ1−γ≤21−γ.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{1-p-\delta}\leq\frac{2\gamma}{1-\gamma}\leq\frac{2}{1-\gamma}.

The conditional expectation bound also holds when the trajectory is not collected, since then Tj=0T_{j}=0. For a history at which trajectory jj is collected, let Qi,j(⋅∣ℱj−1)Q_{i,j}(\cdot\mid\mathcal{F}_{j-1}) denote its conditional law under ℳi\mathcal{M}_{i}, and define:

Kj:=DKL(Q1,j(⋅∣ℱj−1)∥Q2,j(⋅∣ℱj−1)).\displaystyle K_{j}:=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(Q_{1,j}(\cdot\mid\mathcal{F}_{j-1})\,\middle\|\,Q_{2,j}(\cdot\mid\mathcal{F}_{j-1})\right).

We set Kj=0K_{j}=0 at histories where trajectory jj is not collected. Applying the conditional chain rule within a collected trajectory gives:

Kj\displaystyle K_{j} =𝔼𝒜,ℳ1[∑t=0Hj−1DKL(P(1)(⋅∣sj,t,aj,t)∥P(2)(⋅∣sj,t,aj,t))|ℱj−1]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M}_{1}}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{H_{j}-1}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(P^{(1)}(\cdot\mid s_{j,t},a_{j,t})\,\middle\|\,P^{(2)}(\cdot\mid s_{j,t},a_{j,t})\right)\,\middle|\,\mathcal{F}_{j-1}\right]
≤4​δ21−γ​𝔼𝒜,ℳ1​[Tj∣ℱj−1]\displaystyle\leq\frac{4\delta^{2}}{1-\gamma}\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M}_{1}}\left[T_{j}\mid\mathcal{F}_{j-1}\right]
≤8​δ2(1−γ)2.\displaystyle\leq\frac{8\delta^{2}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}.

Therefore, the same upper bound applies to every collected trajectory, uniformly over the preceding history and the algorithm’s policy choices. Finally, applying the conditional chain rule across trajectories yields:

DKL​(ℙ𝒜,ℳ1∥ℙ𝒜,ℳ2)\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M}_{1}}\,\middle\|\,\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M}_{2}}\right)
=∑j=1∞𝔼𝒜,ℳ1[𝟏{N𝒜≥j}Kj]\displaystyle\quad=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M}_{1}}\left[\mathbf{1}_{\{N_{\mathcal{A}}\geq j\}}K_{j}\right]
≤8​δ2(1−γ)2​∑j=1∞ℙ𝒜,ℳ1​(N𝒜≥j)\displaystyle\quad\leq\frac{8\delta^{2}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M}_{1}}(N_{\mathcal{A}}\geq j)
=8​δ2(1−γ)2​𝔼𝒜,ℳ1​[N𝒜]\displaystyle\quad=\frac{8\delta^{2}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M}_{1}}[N_{\mathcal{A}}]
≤8​n​δ2(1−γ)2.\displaystyle\quad\leq\frac{8n\delta^{2}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}.

The chain-rule identities for random trajectory lengths and the complete interaction history follow by padding observations with zeros after termination, applying the chain rule to finite prefixes, and passing to the limit. The algorithm’s internal randomization has the same distribution under both instances, while its action-selection, continuation, and output rules coincide conditional on the same history. Hence, only the environment transition dynamics contribute to the KL divergence.

Part VI: Sample Complexity Lower Bound. Combining the results from Parts IV and V, any algorithm achieving an expected suboptimality gap bounded by ϵ\epsilon on both instances must satisfy,

12≤DKL​(ℙ𝒜,ℳ1∥ℙ𝒜,ℳ2)≤8​n​δ2(1−γ)2.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\leq D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M}_{1}}\,\middle\|\,\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M}_{2}}\right)\leq\frac{8n\delta^{2}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}.

This yields the trajectory budget requirement:

n≥(1−γ)216​δ2.\displaystyle n\geq\frac{(1-\gamma)^{2}}{16\delta^{2}}.

Substituting the perturbation parameter selected in Part III,

δ=64​ϵ​(1−γ)2Rmax​(1−2​α),\displaystyle\delta=\frac{64\epsilon(1-\gamma)^{2}}{R_{\max}(1-2\alpha)},

we obtain:

n\displaystyle n ≥(1−γ)216​Rmax2​(1−2​α)24096​ϵ2​(1−γ)4\displaystyle\geq\frac{(1-\gamma)^{2}}{16}\frac{R_{\max}^{2}(1-2\alpha)^{2}}{4096\epsilon^{2}(1-\gamma)^{4}}
=Rmax2​(1−2​α)265536​ϵ2​(1−γ)2.\displaystyle=\frac{R_{\max}^{2}(1-2\alpha)^{2}}{65536\epsilon^{2}(1-\gamma)^{2}}.

In particular, fixing α=1/4\alpha=1/4 gives:

maxi∈{1,2}⁡𝔼𝒜,ℳi​[N𝒜]≥Rmax2262144​ϵ2​(1−γ)2.\displaystyle\max_{i\in\{1,2\}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M}_{i}}[N_{\mathcal{A}}]\geq\frac{R_{\max}^{2}}{262144\epsilon^{2}(1-\gamma)^{2}}.

Thus, for γ∈[2/3,1)\gamma\in[2/3,1) and

0<ϵ≤Rmax256​γ​(1−γ),\displaystyle 0<\epsilon\leq\frac{R_{\max}}{256\gamma(1-\gamma)},

any algorithm guaranteeing ϵ\epsilon-optimality on both possible unknown instances requires a worst-case expected number of trajectories satisfying

n=Ω⁡(Rmax2(1−γ)2​ϵ2).\displaystyle n=\Omega\!\left(\frac{R_{\max}^{2}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}\epsilon^{2}}\right).

This establishes the claimed trajectory complexity lower bound for adaptive algorithms, including algorithms whose number of collected trajectories is random. ∎

Appendix H Technical Lemmas

Lemma H.1.

Let 𝐆:[0,1]→ℝd\bm{G}:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}^{d} be continuous on [0,1][0,1]. If, for any u∈[0,1)u\in[0,1),

lim supϵ↓0‖𝑮⁡(u+ϵ)−𝑮⁡(u)‖ϵ≤C,\limsup_{\epsilon\downarrow 0}\frac{\|\bm{G}(u+\epsilon)-\bm{G}(u)\|}{\epsilon}\leq C,

then ‖𝐆⁡(1)−𝐆⁡(0)‖≤C\|\bm{G}(1)-\bm{G}(0)\|\leq C.

Proof.

If 𝑮⁡(1)=𝑮⁡(0)\bm{G}(1)=\bm{G}(0) there is nothing to prove, so assume ‖𝑮⁡(1)−𝑮⁡(0)‖>0\|\bm{G}(1)-\bm{G}(0)\|>0. By contradiction, suppose ‖𝑮⁡(1)−𝑮⁡(0)‖>C\|\bm{G}(1)-\bm{G}(0)\|>C and choose c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R} such that ‖𝑮⁡(1)−𝑮⁡(0)‖>c>C\|\bm{G}(1)-\bm{G}(0)\|>c>C. Let

𝒗≔𝑮⁡(1)−𝑮⁡(0)‖𝑮⁡(1)−𝑮⁡(0)‖,\bm{v}\coloneqq\frac{\bm{G}(1)-\bm{G}(0)}{\|\bm{G}(1)-\bm{G}(0)\|},

and define f:[0,1]→ℝf:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R} as f⁡(u)≔𝒗⊤​𝑮​(u)−c​uf(u)\coloneqq\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{G}(u)-cu. Then, f⁡(1)−f⁡(0)=‖𝑮⁡(1)−𝑮⁡(0)‖−c>0f(1)-f(0)=\|\bm{G}(1)-\bm{G}(0)\|-c>0. Since ff is continuous on [0,1][0,1], it attains its minimum at some u⋆∈[0,1]u^{\star}\in[0,1]. Since f⁡(1)>f⁡(0)f(1)>f(0), u⋆<1u^{\star}<1. For sufficiently small ϵ\epsilon, f⁡(u⋆+ϵ)−f⁡(u⋆)≥0f(u^{\star}+\epsilon)-f(u^{\star})\geq 0, so:

lim supϵ↓0f⁡(u⋆+ϵ)−f⁡(u⋆)ϵ≥0.\limsup_{\epsilon\downarrow 0}\frac{f(u^{\star}+\epsilon)-f(u^{\star})}{\epsilon}\geq 0.

On the other hand, since ‖𝒗‖=1\|\bm{v}\|=1,

lim supϵ↓0f⁡(u⋆+ϵ)−f⁡(u⋆)ϵ\displaystyle\limsup_{\epsilon\downarrow 0}\frac{f(u^{\star}+\epsilon)-f(u^{\star})}{\epsilon} =lim supϵ↓0𝒗⊤​(𝑮⁡(u⋆+ϵ)−𝑮⁡(u⋆))ϵ−c\displaystyle=\limsup_{\epsilon\downarrow 0}\frac{\bm{v}^{\top}(\bm{G}(u^{\star}+\epsilon)-\bm{G}(u^{\star}))}{\epsilon}-c
≤lim supϵ↓0‖𝑮⁡(u⋆+ϵ)−𝑮⁡(u⋆)‖ϵ−c\displaystyle\leq\limsup_{\epsilon\downarrow 0}\frac{\|\bm{G}(u^{\star}+\epsilon)-\bm{G}(u^{\star})\|}{\epsilon}-c
≤C−c<0.\displaystyle\leq C-c<0.

∎

Lemma H.2 (Recurrence).

Let {xk}k=0∞\{x_{k}\}_{k=0}^{\infty} be a non-negative sequence satisfying the following recurrence relation for all k≥0k\geq 0:

xk+1≤xk−min⁡{a​xk2,b​xk}+e,\displaystyle x_{k+1}\leq x_{k}-\min\left\{ax_{k}^{2},bx_{k}\right\}+e,

where a>0a>0, b>0b>0, and e>0e>0. For a given target accuracy ϵ>0\epsilon>0, define the effective contraction rate ρϵ≔min⁡{a​ϵ,b}\rho_{\epsilon}\coloneqq\min\{a\epsilon,b\}. Assume the algorithmic parameters are configured such that ρϵ∈(0,1)\rho_{\epsilon}\in(0,1). If the noise term ee satisfies e≤a​ϵ22e\leq a\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{2} and e≤b​ϵ2e\leq b\frac{\epsilon}{2}, then, it suffices to choose a number of iterations KK satisfying:

K≥max⁡{1a​ϵ,1b}​log+⁡(2​x0ϵ),\displaystyle K\geq\max\left\{\frac{1}{a\epsilon},\frac{1}{b}\right\}\log_{+}\left(\frac{2x_{0}}{\epsilon}\right),

where log+⁡(a)≔log⁡max⁡{1,a}\log_{+}(a)\coloneqq\log\max\{1,a\}, to ensure that xk≤ϵx_{k}\leq\epsilon for every k≥Kk\geq K.

Proof.

We first establish that the sequence remains within the target neighborhood once it reaches it. By the stated noise conditions, we have:

e≤min⁡{a​ϵ22,b​ϵ2}=ρϵ​ϵ2.\displaystyle e\leq\min\left\{\frac{a\epsilon^{2}}{2},\frac{b\epsilon}{2}\right\}=\frac{\rho_{\epsilon}\epsilon}{2}.

Suppose that xk≤ϵx_{k}\leq\epsilon. If xk≤ϵ/2x_{k}\leq\epsilon/2, dropping the non-negative descent term yields:

xk+1≤xk+e≤ϵ2+ρϵ​ϵ2≤ϵ,\displaystyle x_{k+1}\leq x_{k}+e\leq\frac{\epsilon}{2}+\frac{\rho_{\epsilon}\epsilon}{2}\leq\epsilon,

where the final inequality follows from ρϵ∈(0,1)\rho_{\epsilon}\in(0,1). Conversely, if ϵ/2<xk≤ϵ\epsilon/2<x_{k}\leq\epsilon, we lower-bound the descent term as follows:

min⁡{a​xk2,b​xk}\displaystyle\min\{ax_{k}^{2},bx_{k}\} =xk​min⁡{a​xk,b}\displaystyle=x_{k}\min\{ax_{k},b\}
≥xk​min⁡{a​ϵ2,b}\displaystyle\geq x_{k}\min\left\{\frac{a\epsilon}{2},b\right\}
≥ρϵ2​xk.\displaystyle\geq\frac{\rho_{\epsilon}}{2}x_{k}.

Substituting this bound into the recurrence gives:

xk+1\displaystyle x_{k+1} ≤(1−ρϵ2)​xk+e\displaystyle\leq\left(1-\frac{\rho_{\epsilon}}{2}\right)x_{k}+e
≤(1−ρϵ2)​ϵ+ρϵ​ϵ2=ϵ.\displaystyle\leq\left(1-\frac{\rho_{\epsilon}}{2}\right)\epsilon+\frac{\rho_{\epsilon}\epsilon}{2}=\epsilon.

Consequently, the target neighborhood [0,ϵ][0,\epsilon] is invariant: if xk≤ϵx_{k}\leq\epsilon at any iteration, then xj≤ϵx_{j}\leq\epsilon for every j≥kj\geq k. We now evaluate the sequence using a hitting-time argument. Let Tϵ:=inf{k≥0∣xk≤ϵ}T_{\epsilon}:=\inf\{k\geq 0\mid x_{k}\leq\epsilon\} denote the first iteration at which the sequence reaches the target accuracy, with inf∅:=+∞\inf\varnothing:=+\infty. If x0≤ϵx_{0}\leq\epsilon, the invariance established above directly guarantees the claim for every iteration. Assume therefore that x0>ϵx_{0}>\epsilon. By the definition of the hitting time, xk>ϵx_{k}>\epsilon for every k<Tϵk<T_{\epsilon}. This allows us to lower-bound the descent rate prior to reaching the target neighborhood. For any k<Tϵk<T_{\epsilon}, factoring out xkx_{k} yields:

min⁡{a​xk2,b​xk}=xk​min​{a​xk,b}≥xk​min​{a​ϵ,b}.\displaystyle\min\left\{ax_{k}^{2},bx_{k}\right\}=x_{k}\min\left\{ax_{k},b\right\}\geq x_{k}\min\left\{a\epsilon,b\right\}.

Substituting the definition of the effective contraction rate ρϵ≔min⁡{a​ϵ,b}\rho_{\epsilon}\coloneqq\min\{a\epsilon,b\} into the original inequality yields a standard linear recurrence:

xk+1≤(1−ρϵ)​xk+e.\displaystyle x_{k+1}\leq(1-\rho_{\epsilon})x_{k}+e.

To set the hyperparameters so that the target xK≤ϵx_{K}\leq\epsilon is reached, we partition the error budget equally, requiring the asymptotic bias to be bounded by ϵ2\frac{\epsilon}{2} and the transient term to be bounded by ϵ2\frac{\epsilon}{2}. Bounding the asymptotic bias requires eρϵ≤ϵ2\frac{e}{\rho_{\epsilon}}\leq\frac{\epsilon}{2}, which rearranges to e≤ρϵ​ϵ2e\leq\rho_{\epsilon}\frac{\epsilon}{2}. Because ρϵ\rho_{\epsilon} evaluates to the minimum of two regimes, this condition must hold for both possible values. If ρϵ=a​ϵ\rho_{\epsilon}=a\epsilon, the constraint dictates e≤a​ϵ22e\leq a\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{2}. If ρϵ=b\rho_{\epsilon}=b, the constraint dictates e≤b​ϵ2e\leq b\frac{\epsilon}{2}. Satisfying both of these stated hyperparameter conditions ensures the asymptotic bias remains strictly bounded by ϵ2\frac{\epsilon}{2}. Consequently, as long as xk≥ϵ>0x_{k}\geq\epsilon>0, we can rewrite the linear recurrence as:

xk+1−ϵ2≤(1−ρϵ)​(xk−ϵ2).\displaystyle x_{k+1}-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\leq(1-\rho_{\epsilon})\left(x_{k}-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\right).

For any integer K<TϵK<T_{\epsilon}, unrolling this recursive inequality over KK steps yields:

xK\displaystyle x_{K} ≤ϵ2+(1−ρϵ)K​(x0−ϵ2)\displaystyle\leq\frac{\epsilon}{2}+(1-\rho_{\epsilon})^{K}\left(x_{0}-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\right)
≤ϵ2+exp⁡(−ρϵ​K)​x0,\displaystyle\leq\frac{\epsilon}{2}+\exp(-\rho_{\epsilon}K)x_{0},

where the final bound applies the standard logarithmic inequality 1−x≤exp⁡(−x)1-x\leq\exp(-x), valid for ρϵ∈(0,1)\rho_{\epsilon}\in(0,1). Bounding the remaining transient term by ϵ/2\epsilon/2 requires:

K\displaystyle K ≥1ρϵ​log+⁡(2​x0ϵ)\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{\rho_{\epsilon}}\log_{+}\left(\frac{2x_{0}}{\epsilon}\right)
=max⁡{1a​ϵ,1b}​log+⁡(2​x0ϵ).\displaystyle=\max\left\{\frac{1}{a\epsilon},\frac{1}{b}\right\}\log_{+}\left(\frac{2x_{0}}{\epsilon}\right).

Fix an integer KK satisfying this bound. If Tϵ>KT_{\epsilon}>K, the preceding estimate gives xK≤ϵx_{K}\leq\epsilon, contradicting the definition of TϵT_{\epsilon}. Hence, Tϵ≤KT_{\epsilon}\leq K. By the invariance of the target neighborhood, it follows that xk≤ϵx_{k}\leq\epsilon for every k≥Kk\geq K, completing the proof. ∎

Appendix I Experimental Details

We evaluate the empirical sample efficiency of the LVR-PG framework on CartPole-v1, Swimmer-v4, HalfCheetah-v4, and Hopper-v4. The experiments have two objectives: (i) to compare the framework’s configurations with GPOMDP (Baxter and Bartlett, 2001) and N-PG-IGT (Fatkhullin et al., 2023), and (ii) to examine sensitivity to the recursive-update parameter α\alpha and refresh probability pp. We first describe the experimental protocol, then present the environment comparisons, the gradient-variability diagnostic, and the hyperparameter studies.

Policies and Implementation

CartPole-v1 uses a softmax policy with two hidden layers of width 44. The continuous-control tasks use Gaussian policies with two hidden layers of width 3232. All hidden layers use tanh\tanh activations, with Xavier-uniform weight initialization and zero biases. Gaussian policies learn a scalar log standard deviation shared across action coordinates, initialized to the values in Table 5.

The experiments use fixed trajectory horizons. Return comparisons and hyperparameter studies use Adam, whereas the gradient-variability diagnostic uses a constant scalar step size. Training and evaluation use separate random-number streams. Evaluation returns are undiscounted and obtained from stochastic-policy rollouts; evaluation trajectories are excluded from the training sample count. For the environment comparisons, each evaluation averages 1010 episodes, with evaluations every 1010 collected training trajectories and at the final updated policy.

Algorithms

We consider DEF-STORM-PG (α>0\alpha>0, p=0p=0), DEF-PAGE-PG (α=0\alpha=0, p>0p>0), and a hybrid configuration (α>0\alpha>0, p>0p>0). The first two are the defensive-IS versions of STORM-PG (Yuan et al., 2020) and PAGE-PG (Gargiani et al., 2022), respectively. In the comparison tables and figures, LVR-PG denotes the best hybrid configuration, hence the configuration of α\alpha and pp that allow LVR-PG to obtain the maximum performance (please refer to Section I.7 to an example of ablation study). The parameter pp determines the probability of refreshing the gradient estimator with NN new trajectories. The parameter α\alpha controls the recursive momentum update; increasing α\alpha therefore reduces the weight of this correction. All three configurations use defensive IS with ξ=0.5\xi=0.5, as suggested by the theory.

We compare these configurations with GPOMDP (Baxter and Bartlett, 2001) and N-PG-IGT Fatkhullin et al. (2023). GPOMDP computes a fresh on-policy gradient estimate at each update. N-PG-IGT combines normalized updates with implicit gradient transport, using neither importance sampling nor second-order information. The algorithms use an average baseline for gradient estimation. Table 6 summarizes the algorithmic settings used in the environment comparisons.

Performance Measures

Learning curves report mean evaluation returns over five independent runs. Shaded regions indicate the estimated standard error of the mean. We summarize performance over the training budget using normalized Area under the Curve (AUC). Higher AUC indicates that high returns are reached earlier and maintained over a larger part of the budget. Table 4 reports the mean AUC and its confidence interval, showing that the momentum-only configuration of LVR-PG performs consistently better than the competitors in almost all the environments.

I.1 CartPole-v1

CartPole-v1 has a four-dimensional state space (𝒮⊂ℝ4\mathcal{S}\subset\mathbb{R}^{4}) and two discrete actions (𝒜={0,1}\mathcal{A}=\{0,1\}). Figure 5 compares the five algorithms using the settings in Tables 5 and 6.

DEF-STORM-PG and LVR-PG reach returns close to the maximum episodic return of 500500 after approximately 10310^{3} trajectories. Both improve more rapidly than GPOMDP and DEF-PAGE-PG. This shows that, empirically, momentum behaves better than probabilistic refreshes. N-PG-IGT attains high returns but exhibits larger training variance.

I.2 Swimmer-v4

Swimmer-v4 is a locomotion task with an eight-dimensional state space (𝒮⊂ℝ8\mathcal{S}\subset\mathbb{R}^{8}) and a two-dimensional action space (𝒜⊂ℝ2\mathcal{A}\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}). The policy controls an articulated swimmer moving through a fluid environment.

Figure 6 shows that DEF-STORM-PG achieves the highest returns over the evaluated training budget. In this environment, the momentum-only configuration of LVR-PG provides the strongest empirical sample efficiency among the tested configurations. While learning faster in the initial part of the training, N-PG-IGT gets stuck in a suboptimal solution around a cumulative reward of 2727.

I.3 HalfCheetah-v4

HalfCheetah-v4 has a 1717-dimensional state space (𝒮⊂ℝ17\mathcal{S}\subset\mathbb{R}^{17}) and a six-dimensional action space (𝒜⊂ℝ6\mathcal{A}\subset\mathbb{R}^{6}). The policy controls the locomotion of an articulated agent.

In Figure 7, DEF-STORM-PG reaches the best return compared to the other algorithms. Again, N-PG-IGT learns faster in the first part of the learning, but early saturates to a lower cumulative reward compared to DEF-STORM-PG. The experiment also shows that DEF-PAGE-PG, and GPOMDP learn slower in the environment, and achieve a lower cumulative return after observing 10510^{5} trajectories.

I.4 Hopper-v4

Hopper-v4 is a locomotion task with an 1111-dimensional state space (𝒮⊂ℝ11\mathcal{S}\subset\mathbb{R}^{11}) and a three-dimensional action space (𝒜⊂ℝ3\mathcal{A}\subset\mathbb{R}^{3}).

Figure 8 shows that DEF-STORM-PG and N-PG-IGT achieve better performance compared to the other algorithms. Again, this shows that momentum updates are empirically more efficient. Here, we see how DEF-PAGE-PG and GPOMDP learn consistently slower than the algorithms that implement momentum, as they start collecting reward after observing 2×1042\times 10^{4} trajectories.

I.5 Gradient-Estimator Variability on CartPole-v1

We complement the return comparisons with a diagnostic of per-trajectory gradient variability on CartPole-v1. For a batch of mkm_{k} trajectories, let 𝐠k,i\mathbf{g}_{k,i} denote the unweighted, baseline-free GPOMDP contribution evaluated at the current policy parameters. We compute the trace of their sample covariance,

𝕍​ar^​(∇^𝜽†​J​(𝜽k))\displaystyle\widehat{\mathbb{V}\text{ar}}\left(\widehat{\nabla}^{\dagger}_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k})\right) =1mk−1​∑i=1mk‖𝐠k,i−𝐠¯k‖22,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{m_{k}-1}\sum_{i=1}^{m_{k}}\left\|\mathbf{g}_{k,i}-\overline{\mathbf{g}}_{k}\right\|_{2}^{2}, 𝐠¯k\displaystyle\overline{\mathbf{g}}_{k} =1mk​∑i=1mk𝐠k,i.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{m_{k}}\sum_{i=1}^{m_{k}}\mathbf{g}_{k,i}.

We plot the mean of log10⁡𝕍​ar^​(∇^𝜽†​J​(𝜽k))\log_{10}\widehat{\mathbb{V}\text{ar}}\left(\widehat{\nabla}^{\dagger}_{\bm{\theta}}J(\bm{\theta}_{k})\right) across independent runs. The contributions are evaluated at the current policy parameters using the batches collected by each algorithm: on-policy batches for GPOMDP and N-PG-IGT, and defensive-mixture batches for the configurations of LVR-PG. Thus, the statistic summarizes the variability of the per-trajectory gradient contributions used in this diagnostic. The experiment uses the configurations of Tables 5 and 6.

Figure 9 shows lower per-trajectory gradient variability for DEF-STORM-PG and the hybrid LVR-PG configuration than for the baselines over much of training. DEF-PAGE-PG also achieves lower values than GPOMDP, while the values for N-PG-IGT increase over the observed budget.

I.6 Hyperparameter Ablations on CartPole-v1

We examine the sensitivity of DEF-PAGE-PG to p∈{0.1,0.5,0.9}p\in\{0.1,0.5,0.9\} and of DEF-STORM-PG to α∈{0.1,0.5,0.9}\alpha\in\{0.1,0.5,0.9\}. Both studies use the CartPole-v1 environment with the configuration presented in Tables 5 and 6.

Figure 10 (left) shows that DEF-PAGE-PG is not much less sensitive to the choice of pp, although frequent refreshes improve its final performance. Both p=0.5p=0.5 and p=0.9p=0.9 reach returns close to 500500, whereas p=0.1p=0.1 settles near 400400. The configuration p=0.9p=0.9 maintains high returns while selecting recursive mini-batch updates with small probability. This suggests that, without momentum, relying heavily on recursive mini-batch updates is less effective in the tested setting. The improvement with more frequent full-batch refreshes is consistent with using larger on-policy batches to control gradient-estimation variance.

Figure 10 (right) shows that DEF-STORM-PG is very sensitive to the choice of α\alpha. The configuration α=0.9\alpha=0.9 rapidly reaches returns close to 500500, while α=0.5\alpha=0.5 requires substantially more trajectories, and α=0.1\alpha=0.1 exhibits persistent fluctuations and lower returns, failing to solve the task in the environment. Thus, a large α\alpha substantially improves empirical sample efficiency in this setting. Since the historical correction is weighted by 1−α1-\alpha, the best-performing configuration retains a smaller correction from the previous estimate.

I.7 Hyperparameter Grid Search for LVR-PG on CartPole-v1

We evaluate hybrid configurations of LVR-PG with α∈{0.01,0.5,0.9}\alpha\in\{0.01,0.5,0.9\} and p∈{0.05,0.3,0.5}p\in\{0.05,0.3,0.5\}. The policy architecture and training settings match the ablation study in Section I.6. Each configuration uses five independent runs. Figure 11 summarizes normalized AUC and terminal return, with terminal return computed as the mean of the last three evaluations in each run.

The grid shows sensitivity to both parameters. At p=0.05p=0.05, increasing α\alpha raises the mean AUC from 12.712.7 to 379.3379.3 and the mean terminal return from 9.39.3 to 336.4336.4. More frequent refreshes substantially improve the low-α\alpha configuration. Three configurations, (0.5,0.3)(0.5,0.3), (0.01,0.5)(0.01,0.5), and (0.9,0.5)(0.9,0.5), attain a mean terminal return of 500500 at the displayed precision, while their mean AUC values differ. The configuration (α,p)=(0.9,0.5)(\alpha,p)=(0.9,0.5) achieves the largest mean AUC in the grid, 453.5±7.2453.5\pm 7.2, combining high terminal performance with the strongest performance over the training budget.

These results identify effective choices within the hybrid configuration and show that its performance depends on the interaction between α\alpha and pp. Together with the experiments presented in Appendix I.6, they motivate selecting DEF-STORM-PG as the primary representative of LVR-PG, since it achieves consistently high mean AUC across the tested environments without periodic full-batch refreshes.
